documents.abstract: .This article proposes a set of media literacy assignments that use generative AI to support critical thinking among future teachers. The study is conceptual and uses a structured analysis of selected academic and UNESCO publications. Six task types are described: distinguishing facts from opinions, checking sources, detecting manipulation, comparing arguments, finding logical gaps, and revising conclusions. For each task, the article identifies a student action, an appropriate AI role, and a simple way to assess the work. The proposed tasks are designed to keep verification and final judgment in the hands of the student. They are offered for future pilot testing and are not presented as proven effective.

The integration of coding and Artificial Intelligence (AI) into vocational education is essential for equipping students with 21st-century digital competencies, yet implementation in remote and island regions like Bangka Belitung archipelago province remains fragmented and unsustainable. This study employs Developmental Evaluation (DE) a real-time, adaptive, and participatory evaluation approach (Patton, 2011) to analyze policy readiness and strengthen the digital ecosystem for coding and AI instruction across vocational schools in the province. Using qualitative methods, including in- depth interviews (n = 26), focus group discussions, classroom observations, and policy document analysis, the research assesses readiness across five core dimensions: (1) policy & governance, (2) human capacity, (3) digital infrastructure, (4) curriculum relevance, and (5) industry–academia partnerships. Findings reveal a critical policy–practice gap: while national frameworks such as the Grand Design for Vocational School Revitalization and Kurikulum Merdeka promote digital literacy, local implementation lacks binding regional regulations, standardized teacher competency pathways, equitable infrastructure distribution, and context-based curricula. Only 24% of ICT teachers had received AI-related training, and AI concepts were rarely taught in practice. Through DE cycles of exploration, collective sense-making, and prototyping, stakeholders co-designed adaptive solutions including a provincial roadmap for digital vocational education, offline AI learning modules via WhatsApp, and micro-innovation grants for teacher-led experimentation. The study demonstrates DE’s effectiveness in fostering adaptive capacity, surfacing systemic barriers, and enabling locally owned, sustainable digital transformation strategies.

Street walkability has both objective and perceived dimensions, yet the extent, spatial distribution, and robustness of mismatches between these assessments remain underexamined. Using central Nanjing, we developed a dual-track framework. The objective track integrated street-network, point-of-interest (POI), and street-view imagery data and used the Criteria Importance Through Intercriteria Correlation (CRITIC) method to construct an objective walkability score (OWS). The perception track used Qwen3-VL-Plus, a multimodal large language model (MLLM), to evaluate street-view images across six dimensions (safety, lively, beautiful, wealthy, depressing, and boring), producing a perceived walkability score (PWS). Model ratings were compared with human ratings for 500 images. Agreement was estimated on those same images, with no independent validation set, and may therefore be optimistic. Pearson correlations across the six dimensions ranged from 0.37 to 0.71. The original-scale composite PWS had an intraclass correlation coefficient of 0.60 and a mean absolute error of 0.85. High-value areas of OWS and PWS did not coincide, and the standardised perception gap score (PGS) remained spatially clustered at both the sampling-point and street-segment levels (Moran's I = 0.306 and 0.247, respectively; permutation p = 0.001 for both). Exploratory geographically weighted regression (GWR) estimated spatial variation in associations between built-environment indicators and PWS. Relative OWS and PWS levels classified sampling points into four diagnostic types, two of them defined by divergence between the assessments. By quantifying and locating the spatial mismatch between objective and perceived walkability, the framework provides diagnostic evidence for incorporating visual perception into fine-grained street-renewal assessment.

Digital transformation has reshaped the professional landscape through the increasing use of artificial intelligence, big data, and social media, while simultaneously generating ethical challenges, including technology misuse, privacy violations, and disinformation. This study aims to examine the role of professional codes of ethics in addressing digital ethical challenges through the perspective of maqāṣid al-sharī‘ah. Employing a qualitative approach, the study combines a literature review with case analysis, including the scandal involving the Community Vocational Training Center (Balai Latihan Kerja Komunitas/BLKK) of the Islamic Scholars Association (PP) in Pekalongan City. The findings indicate that professional codes of ethics function not merely as normative instruments governing professional conduct but also as mechanisms for protecting public welfare in accordance with the objectives of maqāṣid al-sharī‘ah, particularly ḥifẓ al-‘aql (protection of intellect), ḥifẓ al-māl (protection of wealth), ḥifẓ al-‘irḍ (protection of dignity), and ḥifẓ al-nafs (protection of life). The implementation of professional codes of ethics through strengthened digital ethics literacy, professional oversight, and technology-responsive regulatory reform can prevent harm, enhance accountability, and sustain public trust. The findings of this study contribute to proposing the integration of professional codes of ethics with maqāṣid al-sharī‘ah as an adaptive ethical framework for strengthening professionalism in the digital era.

Centralized testing systems routinely build test blueprints on the assumption that an item’s targeted cognitive level, coded with Bloom’s revised taxonomy, is monotonically related to its empirical difficulty and discrimination: lower-order items should be easier, and higher-order items harder and more discriminating. This assumption is rarely tested empirically in K–12 national assessment, and almost never at scale in mathematics. Using item-analysis records for 265 four-option multiple-choice items drawn from centralized mathematics examinations (End-of-Term 1, 2025 2026) across Grades 4–12 and both the General and Advanced tracks, this study examined (a) the alignment between the expert human cognitive classification and the empirical psychometric behaviour of items, and (b) the agreement between the expert classification and an independent large-language-model (LLM) classification produced by Claude (Anthropic). Difficulty (p-value) differed significantly across cognitive bands (Kruskal–Wallis H = 11.26, p = .004), with higher-order items being the hardest; the effect, however, was weak (ε² = .043; Spearman ρ = −.16), and a Jonckheere Terpstra test confirmed a significant decreasing trend across the ordered bands (J = 7943, z = −2.56, p = .006). Discrimination did not differ across cognitive bands (H = 0.54, p = .77), and difficulty and discrimination were essentially uncorrelated (ρ = −.05). Human–AI agreement was only fair (Cohen’s κ = .22 at the six-level resolution and κ = .17 at the three-band level; raw agreement was 51.7% and 58.1%, respectively), with the model systematically over-assigning the “apply/analyse” band. No significant item-level difference emerged between the General and Advanced tracks. The findings offer partial, weak empirical support for the cognitive-difficulty assumption, no support for a cognitive–discrimination link, and a clear caution against replacing expert human coders with current LLMs in high-stakes item classification. Implications for blueprint validation, item-writer training, and AI-assisted assessment workflows are discussed.

Abstract Extracting and formatting data is among the most tedious elements of assessing environmental chemical occurrence and exposure. We present a toolkit (eData) to streamline this process, generate FAIR data, and maximise traceability and transparency: a FAIR Data Reporting Format (DRF) that provides data structure, vocabulary, and validation, and a Large Language Model (LLM)-based data extraction application that quickly formats literature data. Data and metadata for a study of interest can be rapidly extracted to the eData format by a range of commercially available LLMs, and visualised for checking in the application's graphical interface. This blends advantages of LLM extraction with human interpretation, speeding extraction without impairing reproducibility. Data can be exported from the application at any point in this process and saved locally. Furthermore, the application supports a streamlined Criteria for Reporting and Evaluating Exposure Datasets (CREED) data quality assessments that automatically compiles data relevant to the assessment for reporting. All resulting data can also be uploaded to the repository service Zenodo via a dedicated module. Our evaluation showed a substantial time saving per paper (from 3+ to around 1 hour) and extracted consistent data, passing 85% of format validation checks. Our toolkit is a valuable addition to the FAIRification of environmental chemical occurrence and exposure data.

Mathematical problem-solving is a crucial 21st-century competency, yet it remains challenging for elementary school students, particularly in Riau Province. This quantitative experimental study investigated the effectiveness of integrating artificial intelligence (AI) into Quizizz to enhance students’ mathematical problem-solving skills with a Higher Order Thinking Skills (HOTS) orientation. The participants were 64 fourth-grade students at SDN 002 Pasir Limau Kapas, equally assigned to an experimental group (n = 32) using Quizizz AI Quiz Generator and Adaptive Feedback, and a control group (n = 32) using conventional non-AI digital quizzes. Data were obtained through a validated and reliable standardized essay test based on Polya’s four problem-solving stages: understanding the problem, planning a solution, executing the plan, and reviewing the answer. The instrument demonstrated high reliability (Cronbach’s Alpha = 0.86). Data analysis involved descriptive statistics, an independent-samples t-test, and Normalized Gain (N-Gain). The experimental group obtained a significantly higher post-test mean (84.25 ± 7.12) than the control group (69.50 ± 8.45; p < 0.001). The experimental group also achieved a higher N-Gain score (0.71) than the control group (0.42). These findings indicate that AI-supported Quizizz effectively enhances elementary students’ mathematical problem-solving abilities through adaptive and interactive learning.

This study examined the effect of AI-powered skills on learning outcomes of ND/HND Accountancy students in Financial Accounting in Waziri Umaru Federal Polytechnic, Birnin Kebbi, Nigeria. The study adopted quasi-experimental research design of pre-test post-test non-equivalent control group. Two research questions and one null hypothesis guided the study. The population comprised 210 ND II Accountancy students offering ACC 211 (Financial Accounting I) in 2024/2025 academic session. A sample of 60 students was selected using purposive sampling and assigned to experimental group (30 students) and control group (30 students). The experimental group was taught Company Accounts and Final Accounts using AI-powered skills such as ChatGPT for explaining accounting concepts and adjustments, Microsoft 365 Copilot in Excel for automated preparation of Trial Balance, Trading, Profit and Loss Account and Balance Sheet, and Grammarly for audit report writing. Control group was taught using conventional lecture method. The instrument for data collection was Financial Accounting Achievement Test (FAAT) consisting of 30 multiple choice and theory questions covering Company Accounts, Final Accounts, Depreciation, Provision for Bad Debts, Accruals and Prepayments. FAAT was validated by three experts (2 Accountancy, 1 Measurement and Evaluation) and reliability of 0.82 obtained using Kuder-Richardson 20 (KR-20). Mean and standard deviation were used to answer research questions while t-test was used to test hypothesis at 0.05 level of significance. Findings revealed that experimental group had higher post-test mean score of 68.45 (SD=8.21) than control group mean of 51.20 (SD=9.45), with mean gain of 34.25 for experimental and 17.40 for control. The t-test result showed t-calculated of 4.87 greater than t-critical of 2.00 at degree of freedom 58, p<0.05, indicating significant difference. Therefore, AI-powered skills significantly improved learning outcomes of ND/HND Accountancy students in Financial Accounting. It was recommended that lecturers should integrate AI tools into teaching of financial accounting and other accounting courses such as Cost Accounting and Taxation. Workshops should be organized for Accountancy lecturers on AI integration.

The growing prevalence of chronic wound infections presents a major global healthcare challenge due to delayed healing, prolonged hospitalization, and increased rates of limb amputation. Conventional diagnostic approaches, including clinical assessment, microbiological culture, and laboratory-based analyses, are often limited by subjective interpretation, delayed turnaround times, invasive sampling, and an inability to continuously monitor the dynamic wound microenvironment. Because wound infection involves changes in both host physiology and microbial activity, reliance on a single biomarker may not adequately characterize wound status, highlighting the potential of multimodal point-of-care diagnostic platforms. Recent advances in wearable biosensors, surface-enhanced Raman spectroscopy (SERS), nanomaterials, and artificial intelligence (AI) have supported the development of multimodal approaches for monitoring complementary host- and pathogen-derived biomarkers to facilitate rapid, non-invasive, and continuous wound infection assessment. This review examines selected multimodal biosensing approaches for wound infection detection, with a focus on electrochemical biosensors, SERS, and AI-assisted data analytics within point-of-care diagnostic frameworks. The review discusses (1) key wound infection biomarkers and the fundamental principles of electrochemical and SERS-based sensing; (2) recent developments in multimodal biosensing platforms, advanced plasmonic materials, and AI-assisted data interpretation and multimodal data fusion; and (3) current challenges and future opportunities for the clinical translation of point-of-care wound diagnostics. By combining complementary sensing modalities with AI-driven data analytics, these approaches may support earlier infection detection, continuous non-invasive monitoring, personalized wound management, and more informed clinical decision-making.

Abstract Synthetic biology enables the installation of programable genetic functions in microorganisms, positioning them as versatile platforms for therapeutic applications. However, clinical translation requires chassis organisms that integrate safety, genetic stability, and precise control over the activity. Here, we present an innovative engineering framework for the probiotic Escherichia coli Nissle (EcN) that transforms EcN into a safe, efficient, and non-proliferative chassis for therapeutic production. The native EcN plasmids pM1 and pM2 were cured and repurposed to encode two functional modules: a CRISPR-Cas12 chromosome-shredding device that prevents bacterial propagation and a programable circuit for payload expression, thereby generating a non-proliferative therapeutic-producing system. To broaden the range of therapeutic payloads, we developed an artificial-intelligence-guided bioinformatic pipeline to predict anticancer cell-penetrating peptides (ACCPPs). As a proof of concept, a candidate identified through this workflow was produced in the engineered EcN chassis and evaluated in human cell culture for anticancer activity. Collectively, this strategy established a modular platform that integrates computational therapeutic discovery with engineered probiotic production, paving the way for the future development of safer microbial therapies and their clinical applications.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is creating new opportunities for English language teaching through personalized learning, interactive practice, automated feedback, and instructional material development. However, its effective integration requires pedagogical planning, digital competence, and attention to ethical considerations. These issues are particularly relevant to English language education in Uzbekistan, where teachers work in diverse educational settings.

Machine Reading Comprehension (MRC) has become a key benchmark for evaluating natural language processing systems, and multiple-choice question answering is widely adopted for assessing reasoning, comprehension, and commonsense inference capabilities. However, traditional embedding-based approaches often struggle with complex reasoning and have limited access to external knowledge. Although Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong language understanding and reasoning abilities, relying on a single model remains challenging because of hallucinations, model biases, and differences in training data, architectures, and domain expertise. Consequently, no single model consistently performs best across diverse multiple-choice question answering tasks. To address these limitations, we propose an ensemble framework for multiple-choice question answering. The framework incorporates a model selection mechanism that identifies model combinations with complementary error patterns to improve the error-correction capability of the ensemble. In addition, when disagreements occur among the selected base models, a Thinking Model is dynamically invoked to resolve conflicting predictions, thereby reserving advanced reasoning for cases requiring additional resolution. We evaluate nine open-source LLMs on five datasets in Chinese and English. Each dataset is partitioned into 30% validation data for model selection and 70% held-out test data for final evaluation, with the experiment independently repeated five times. Experimental results show that the proposed framework outperforms the individual LLMs on five datasets and achieves an average error-rate reduction ranging from 3.46% to 7.14% relative to conventional ensemble baselines. Furthermore, the proposed approach reduces the average number of Thinking Model invocations by 87.83% compared with the strongest benchmark model while maintaining comparable accuracy, demonstrating a favorable accuracy–efficiency trade-off.

Background Chiselling involves repetitive, precision work with constrained postures and high hand loads, contributing to upper-limb musculoskeletal disorders among artisans. Despite extensive work on workstation ergonomics and general hand-tool design, few studies have systematically translated ergonomic risk-assessment findings into specific chisel-handle design requirements and evaluated the resulting intervention in a real craft-sector setting. Objective This study aimed to characterize ergonomic exposures in chiselling, translate these findings to concrete handle design requirements, and evaluate a prototype handle's short-term usability versus conventional handles. Methods Fifty male artisans underwent NMQ, palm pain mapping, RULA and ART assessment. Risk findings informed a modular ergonomic handle (elliptical contour, 25–40 mm diameter, 10–15° cant, strike ferrule). A counterbalanced in-lab within-subject short-term usability comparison (n = 30) was conducted alongside post-trial acute hand pain mapping and targeted ART posture sub-component reassessment. Results A high prevalence of upper-limb musculoskeletal symptoms and dominant-hand biomechanical risk were identified. The prototype was strongly preferred and rated easier and more comfortable to use, and it markedly reduced acute pain at the thumb base and first finger-web. Usability improved across all items and acute thenar/first-web pain fell substantially (Zones 19–20, paired d > 2.9), with parallel reductions in the wrist-posture and force-demand sub-components of the ART assessment. Conclusions Risk-informed handle redesign yielded immediate, objectively corroborated hand-level benefits. The study contributes a low-cost, retrofittable ergonomic chisel handle and replicable risk-to-design pathway applicable to woodworking artisans and similar occupations. Longitudinal field validation is necessary to establish sustained reductions in musculoskeletal disorder prevalence and productivity gains.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly presented as a tool for sustainable development, yet the ethical costs of this role remain scattered across separate bodies of literature. This systematic review aims to identify the ethical issues arising at the intersection of AI, ethics, and sustainability. Following the preferred reporting items for systematic reviews and meta-analyses 2020 statement, Scopus and Web of Science were searched in February 2026, yielding 5,794 records. Screening, eligibility assessment and quality appraisal were carried out by two researchers, and 74 studies were included. Verbatim passages addressing the intersection were extracted from each study and examined using a hybrid thematic approach, resulting in 921 coded passages. Five themes were identified: algorithmic bias and unequal AI outcomes; privacy, surveillance, and human autonomy; transparency, accountability, and epistemic integrity; AI governance and corporate responsibility; and the ecological ethics of AI systems. Concerns regarding transparency and accountability accounted for the largest share of passages (30.9%), while ecological concerns were voiced across all five themes rather than in a separate discussion. The themes were mapped onto the environmental, social, and governance dimensions of sustainability and onto the United Nations sustainable development goals. Transparency and accountability thus emerge as a structural prerequisite rather than a procedural add-on for sustainable AI. Educational research is markedly underrepresented at this intersection (5 of 74 studies); the implications of the five themes for science, mathematics, and technology education are therefore developed in detail, from carbon- and water-footprint modelling tasks to data-justice and AI-literacy work in the classroom.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has evolved from speculative theory to a transformative global technology with insightful ethical, social, and legal implications. In Muslim contexts, the framework of maqāṣid al-sharīʿah - the higher objectives of Islamic law - offers a rich, value-oriented approach to evaluating and guiding the development of AI. It highlights both opportunities and risks across key domains such as healthcare, online content moderation, surveillance, and economic displacement. Acknowledging that AI has emerged as one of the most unsettling technologies of the twenty-first century with its attendant global transformative capacity, its implications for societies like Nigeria, where religious, cultural, and ethical frameworks shape governance and social order, remain underexplored. This article examines the revolution of AI in Nigeria through the lens of Maqāṣid al-Sharīʿah (the higher objectives of Islamic law). Drawing on classical Islamic jurisprudence and contemporary AI debates, the study analyzes how AI aligns with or threatens the preservation of religion (ḥifẓ al-dīn), life (ḥifẓ al-nafs), intellect (ḥifẓ al-ʿaql), lineage (ḥifẓ al-nasl), and property (ḥifẓ al-māl). It argues that Nigeria’s engagement with AI must not only reflect global ethical principles but also incorporate indigenous religious traditions to ensure justice, human dignity, and social welfare. The article concludes with maqāṣid-based policy recommendations to guide Nigeria’s AI future.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Forecasting the direction and magnitude of stock price movements remains one of the most persistently difficult problems in applied machine learning, owing to the noisy, non-stationary, and weak-form-efficient character of financial time series. This survey examines three recent studies that approach the problem through complementary lenses: an explainable Decision Tree that builds dynamic, industry-specific lexicons from financial news to classify next-day price-change magnitude [1]; a feature-engineering and portfolio-construction pipeline that derives new price-based predictors via Principal Component Analysis (PCA), Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA), and a proposed Statistical Average Method (SAM) before applying eight regression architectures, including Bi-LSTM [2]; and an LSTM-based trend classifier that fuses FinBERT-scored Twitter sentiment with price data to forecast North American and European bank-stock movements during the macroeconomically turbulent year of 2022 [3]. Beyond summarising each study's objectives, methodology, data, and results, this survey situates the three works within the broader and rapidly evolving literature on deep sequence models (LSTM, Bi-LSTM, GRU, and transformer architectures), sentiment analysis with pretrained financial language models such as FinBERT, and explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) in finance. A structured comparative analysis contrasts the three studies along ten dimensions, including data sources, feature engineering, model architecture, explainability, validation design, and reported performance, while explicitly cautioning against directly ranking studies whose prediction tasks and evaluation metrics are not commensurable. A cross-domain case study of an attention-based legislative-vote predictor is retained to examine whether a learned similarity mechanism could improve on the fixed similarity rules used throughout the finance literature reviewed here. The survey's contribution lies in bringing explainable lexicon-based methods, statistically engineered price features, and sentiment-driven deep learning together within a single comparative framework, and in using that synthesis to identify concrete, evidence-grounded gaps around auxiliary-signal fusion, the explainability of high-accuracy sequence models, and cross-market generalisation.

Abstract Recent developments of Artificial Intelligence of Things (AIoT) are transforming several sectors like Industry 4.0, smart cities, intelligent healthcare, and smart transportation. The AIoT can be employed in urban mobility to enable real-time monitoring and intelligent decision-making in the transportation sector. Traffic congestion classification is a significant aspect of Intelligent Transportation Systems (ITS), as the rising urban population has contributed to severe congestion complexity that impacts air quality, road safety, and travel time. Accurate classification of congestion patterns improves traffic management and mitigates environmental impacts. Although precisely predicting congestion spread is still problematic, owing to the complex, non-linear, and dynamic nature of traffic patterns. As deep learning advances, efficient models are required to address the challenges in smart urban mobility systems. Therefore, this study presents a Deep Learning-Based Urban Mobility Intelligent System for Traffic Congestion Framework (DLUMIS-TCF). The proposed DLUMIS-TCF model analyzes urban mobility data with trip-level records for precise traffic congestion level classification. The preprocessing stage includes missing value handling, outlier detection, feature scaling, temporal attribute extraction, and spatial coordinate utilization to prepare the data for effective learning. For feature selection, the model utilizes Elastic Net to select the relevant spatio-temporal features from the dataset. In addition, the traffic congestion level classification is performed using a heterogeneous spatiotemporal graph attention network. Furthermore, the optimization of the model is carried out using the AdaBelief optimizer to improve convergence and performance. To improve the interpretability of the model, SHAP is used to explain the contribution of input features toward the classification results. To assess the performance of the proposed DLUMIS-TCF model, experiments are carried out on an Urban Mobility Intelligence Dataset obtained from the Kaggle repository. The experimental results show the effectiveness of the proposed model in predicting traffic congestion compared to other methods. Thus, the proposed DLUMIS-TCF approach can be useful for urban traffic management, congestion control, and intelligent transportation systems.

Background: Precision laboratory diagnosis increasingly relies on the interpretation of heterogeneous biological and clinical information. Conventional workflows tend to examine biomarkers, molecular measurements, immunological findings, and clinical characteristics along partly separate analytical pathways. Artificial intelligence (AI) can uncover complex relationships in high-dimensional biomedical data, yet many such systems remain hard to interpret at the point of clinical use. Explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) renders algorithmic outputs more transparent by identifying the features, modalities, and interactions that shape a prediction. Objective: This manuscript proposes an explainable multimodal AI framework for precision laboratory diagnosis, termed XMAI-PLD, which unites conventional laboratory biomarkers, molecular profiles, immunological signatures, and clinical data within a single analytical architecture. The framework is designed to support, rather than supplant, laboratory expertise and clinical judgement. Framework: The architecture comprises seven interconnected layers: data acquisition; quality control and harmonisation; modality-specific representation; multimodal fusion; diagnostic inference; explainability and uncertainty assessment; and laboratory–clinical decision support. Biomarker measurements contribute quantitative biochemical information, molecular profiles characterise genomic or molecular alterations, immunological signatures capture host-response patterns, and clinical variables supply patient-level context. Each stream is processed separately before being integrated through multimodal learning, and explanations are generated at the modality and feature levels to reveal the principal drivers of each output. Clinical and Laboratory Relevance: The framework addresses the shortcomings of isolated single-modality models, namely incomplete biological representation, heterogeneous data structures, missing information, analytical variability, and limited interpretability. Its proposed outputs comprise diagnostic probabilities, contributing features, modality-level evidence, uncertainty estimates, and cases flagged for human review. Particular emphasis falls on analytical validity, calibration, external validation, data provenance, subgroup assessment, cybersecurity, privacy, and human oversight. Conclusion: Explainable multimodal AI offers a promising route towards a more integrated diagnostic representation of laboratory and clinical evidence. Its worth will hinge not only on predictive performance but also on analytical robustness, reproducibility, interpretability, calibration, clinical usefulness, and sustained human oversight. Prospective, multicentre evaluation is required before such systems enter routine diagnostic practice.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Objective: The present study aimed to explain FOMO (Fear of Missing Out) symptoms based on maladaptive perfectionism and emotional loneliness, with a particular focus on the mediating role of artificial intelligence dependency among female high school adolescents. Methods and Materials: This correlational study employed a structural equation modeling approach to investigate the relationships among maladaptive perfectionism, emotional loneliness, artificial intelligence dependency, and FOMO symptoms. The statistical population consisted of all female students enrolled in secondary high schools in Dezful, Iran, during the 2025–2026 academic year. A total of 250 students were selected through convenience sampling. Data were collected using the Fear of Missing Out Scale developed by Przybylski et al. (2013), the Multidimensional Perfectionism Questionnaire by Hewitt and Flett (2004), the Social and Emotional Loneliness Scale by DiTommaso et al. (2004), and the Artificial Intelligence Dependency Questionnaire developed by Huang et al. (2024). Data analysis was conducted using descriptive and inferential statistics in SPSS and AMOS software packages. Path analysis and structural equation modeling were utilized to evaluate both direct and indirect relationships among the study variables and to assess the overall model fit. Findings: The results demonstrated that maladaptive perfectionism and emotional loneliness significantly predicted FOMO symptoms both directly and indirectly through artificial intelligence dependency. Maladaptive perfectionism showed a significant positive effect on artificial intelligence dependency (β = 0.411, p < .01), while emotional loneliness also exhibited a significant positive effect on artificial intelligence dependency (β = 0.506, p < .01). Furthermore, maladaptive perfectionism had a significant direct effect on FOMO symptoms (β = 0.267, p < .01) and a significant indirect effect through artificial intelligence dependency (β = 0.124, p < .01). Similarly, emotional loneliness exerted a significant direct effect on FOMO symptoms (β = 0.259, p < .01) and a significant indirect effect mediated by artificial intelligence dependency (β = 0.152, p < .01). Artificial intelligence dependency itself significantly and positively predicted FOMO symptoms (β = 0.301, p < .01). Model fit indices indicated a satisfactory fit of the proposed structural model to the observed data. Conclusion: The findings suggest that adolescents with higher levels of maladaptive perfectionism and emotional loneliness are more likely to develop dependency on artificial intelligence technologies, which in turn intensifies FOMO symptoms. Artificial intelligence dependency functions as a significant psychological mechanism linking individual vulnerabilities and social-emotional difficulties to heightened fear of missing out. These results highlight the importance of addressing maladaptive perfectionistic standards, strengthening real-world emotional relationships, and promoting healthy patterns of AI use in interventions designed to reduce FOMO among adolescents.

BackgroundThe integration of artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) within the clinical work of rehabilitation therapists in post stroke rehabilitation has the potential to transform their work performance, habits, and routines. The impact could potentially enhance integration of assessment/data analysis, personalizing therapies, documentation, and promoting home program adherence.ObjectiveThis study assesses occupational and physical therapists' current perspectives on AI/ML in post-stroke clinical rehabilitation and examines perceived barriers to potential application of AI/ML in their clinical work.MethodsThis mixed methods study includes quantitative survey data collected pre/post an AI/ML educational webinar, as well as qualitative focus group analysis that includes therapist attitudes and experiences with AI/ML, practical applications to using AI/ML, as well as the difficulties associated. The recruited therapists include occupational and physical therapy practitioners from the United States and Asia. Individuals included in the study had to have a caseload of 30% persons with stroke.ResultsFour key themes emerged from qualitative analysis: 1) current clinical work practice and identified gaps, 2) current therapists' perceptions of AI/ML, 3) perceived future of AI/ML in clinical work practices and 4) steps needed for implementation. Survey data reporting frequencies of technology use and AI/ML perceptions are integrated into qualitative findings.ConclusionsTherapists can articulate potential future uses for AI/ML technology in post-stroke rehabilitation, however, remain uncertain about when, how, and at what cost utilization will be supported in clinical work environments. Therapists desire education and support to utilize the evolving technologies in practice.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Purpose This paper examines the ethical and epistemological implications of language generated by large language models (LLMs) through the lenses of speech act theory, conversational implicature and second-order cybernetics. LLMs are often presented as neutral tools, yet their outputs actively participate in shaping discourse in ways that carry consequences for meaning, responsibility and pluralism. Design/methodology/approach The paper introduces the concept of soft derogation to describe a form of linguistic exclusion, one that operates through euphemization, omission and the simulation of neutrality rather than overt offense. Such processes can subtly promote or suppress certain ideas, values or identities without transparent authorship or intention. The result is a shift toward an algorithmically generated form of newspeak, where expressive possibilities are narrowed through alignment protocols and safety layers. Findings Drawing on second-order cybernetics, the paper argues that ethical responsibility for AI-generated language is distributed across developers, deployers, institutional stakeholders and human interpreters. While users co-construct meaning within recursive socio-technical systems, the upstream actors who design alignment protocols, moderation layers and deployment conditions bear primary responsibility for the communicative environments they create. Originality/value Relatively little work has examined how the pertinent philosophical frameworks can illuminate forms of linguistic influence that operate through euphemization, omission and simulated neutrality. This paper addresses that gap by analyzing how algorithmically generated language can shape discourse while appearing neutral.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Background Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) adoption transformed work structures after 2022, raising psychological safety concerns as efficiency priorities overshadow human-centered employee wellbeing. Objective This longitudinal study investigates how engagement is framed as a corporate communication strategy in Standard & Poor's (S&P) 500 technology firms during early large-scale AI adoption (2022–2024). Methods Using IRaMuTeQ, 150 S&P 500 corporate reports (2022–2024) underwent Reinert's Descending Hierarchical Classification, Correspondence Factorial Analysis, and similarity network analysis, employing chi-square ( χ 2 ) marker filtering. Results Findings reveal a three-stage trajectory mapping onto dynamic capabilities: initial sensing (2022), platform seizing (2023), and process transformation (2024). However, human-centered engagement language (meaningfulness, safety, vigor) remained structurally marginalized, failing to form a stable lexical cluster and framing participation strictly through technical integration. Conclusions Public discourse serves as a proxy for enacting dynamic capabilities. Practically, HR leaders should prospectively audit AI communications to ensure technical efficiency narratives do not displace human-centered and psychological safety registers.

Artificial intelligence requires systematic reflection on the relationship between technological progress, collective responsibility and the dignity of the person, making a new social pact necessary. The article links dependence on fossil fuels to geopolitical imbalances, inflationary pressures and the ability of authoritarian regimes to support power policies, proposing international coordination, including at the UN, that reconciles energy security, climate protection and the transition to renewable sources and, in perspective, nuclear fusion. This analysis is accompanied by the criticism of an economy based exclusively on solvency, which excludes needs without adequate purchasing power from the production and distribution of essential goods. To combat poverty, inequality and vulnerability to war, an international agency capable of promoting socially useful work and coordinating the production and distribution of fundamental resources is envisaged. In this framework, artificial intelligence and robotics could contribute to the analysis of needs, the organization of work, agriculture, assistance and scientific research, as long as they remain subordinate to democratic decision-making and criteria of transparency, human control and non-discrimination. Finally, the technological comparison between the United States, China and Europe shows the need, especially for Europe, to strengthen investment, research and regulatory capacity. Energy, peace, social justice and innovation are thus brought back to the different dimensions of a single pact based on collective responsibility and human dignity.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Abstract Whether a new technology needs its own law is an old question, and for artificial intelligence (AI), it has been posed at the wrong level of abstraction. Both the case against technology-specific law and the case for regulation by design treat the AI model as the regulated object, although a general-purpose model acquires its risk only when deployed. This article relocates the regulatory object to the deployment workflow, defined as the envelope of thresholds, escalation pathways and human checkpoints that surrounds a model in use, and reads the EU Artificial Intelligence Act as management-based regulation that works only where the workflow is specifiable and a standing supervisor examines it. Hungary’s first-wave implementation shows the second condition deciding the outcome: the same obligations are supervised by the central bank in finance and by a ministry with no examination relationship in employment, so the Act’s uniform text conceals uneven supervision within one Member State. The Digital Omnibus on AI, which postpones the high-risk obligations because standards and authorities are late, opens a window to build supervision deliberately: the priority is not better definitions but better supervision.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) weakens a practical assumption in the European Credit Transfer and Accumulation System (ECTS): that estimated student workload remains a credible proxy for learning when assessment evidence is interpretable. This conceptual article examines what follows when academic products are routinely produced through hybrid human–AI cognition. Drawing on Kane’s interpretation/use argument, assessment-security scholarship and recent work on GenAI in higher education, it reconstructs ECTS as an inferential system in which scores, generalisation, extrapolation and credit-awarding uses must all be warranted. The analysis shows that opaque take-home production can weaken each link: scoring may misread distributed authorship, generalisation becomes unstable, extrapolation to learning outcomes is less secure, and credit awards risk retaining administrative form without evidential force. The article proposes verified learning as a credit-level validity condition and specifies four safeguards: programme-level alignment, authentic transfer tasks, process visibility with declared AI use, and strategic controlled verification. It also identifies equity and governance conditions required for these safeguards to support, rather than undermine, comparability across ECTS-based institutions in AI-rich assessment environments. The contribution is to connect task-level assessment validity to credit legitimacy and to translate that connection into practical design and quality-assurance implications for European higher education policy.

topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: ABSTRACT The adoption of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is reshaping the very nature of work, yet its social meaning and evaluative implications—particularly for women—remain underexplored. Although existing research has mainly examined GenAI adoption, use, and algorithmic bias, less is known about how the use of GenAI shapes how individuals are evaluated by others. Drawing on the Stereotype Content Model, Role Congruity Theory and techno‐feminism perspectives, this study examines how women's use of GenAI influences perceptions of competence and warmth in academia. Using a 2 × 2 × 2 experimental vignette design [gender*GenAI adoption*task type (teaching vs. research)] with 651 participants, we examine how evaluations vary by academic gender, GenAI adoption, and task domain (teaching vs. research). We find that GenAI adoption generally enhances perceived competence. Women, however, gain the most in research tasks, where technical skills challenge gendered expectations. Conversely, GenAI use reduces perceived warmth, disproportionately penalizing women, especially in research. These findings reveal a “double bind,” highlighting how GenAI adoption may reproduce and intensify gendered evaluative tradeoffs within academic prestige hierarchies and the need for institutional strategies to mitigate relational penalties while recognizing competence.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: The increasing adoption of Generative Artificial Intelligence (Generative AI) is transforming the nature of work, employee roles and human resource management practices across organisations. Deposit Money Banks are particularly affected because their operations involve extensive information processing, customer interaction, documentation, decision support and knowledge-intensive activities. However, the extent to which Generative AI contributes to employee productivity may depend on how effectively organisations manage workforce transformation. This study examined the relationship between Generative AI and workforce transformation and proposed an AI-HRM framework for improving employee productivity in Deposit Money Banks operating in Rivers State. The study specifically examined the relationships between Generative AI and employee reskilling, job redesign, human–AI collaboration and employee productivity. A cross-sectional correlational research design was adopted. Data were collected from employees of selected Deposit Money Banks operating in Rivers State using a structured questionnaire. Reliability was confirmed using Cronbach’s Alpha coefficients above 0.70. Out of 344 questionnaire administered, 300 usable copies were retrieved and use for the analysis with the aid of SPSS version 27.0. The findings suggest that Generative AI should not be viewed merely as a replacement for human labour but as a technology capable of augmenting employees’ capabilities and transforming the way work is organised and performed. The study therefore proposed an AI-HRM framework based on AI readiness, Generative AI adoption, employee reskilling, job redesign, human–AI collaboration and productivity improvement. The study concludes that Deposit Money Banks can achieve greater productivity benefits from Generative AI when its adoption is supported by appropriate HRM practices, continuous employee development and effective human–AI collaboration. The study contributes to knowledge by providing a context-specific AI-HRM framework for managing workforce transformation and improving employee productivity in Deposit Money Banks operating in Rivers State.
topics: Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society

documents.abstract: Background. Generative artificial intelligence (generative AI) tools have diffused rapidly into university study, yet, in the literature reviewed for this study, most empirical evidence concerns designed interventions or Western student populations. How students in Southeast Asia draw on these tools in unsupervised, self-directed academic work is sparsely documented in that literature. Objective. This exploratory study describes self-reported generative AI use, perceived effectiveness, and the benefits and concerns articulated by university students, primarily in Indonesia. Methods. A cross-sectional online survey was administered via Google Forms in June 2026. Twenty-four students accessed the survey; one declined consent, yielding 23 analysable cases (21 Indonesian, 2 Chinese). The instrument comprised seven usagefrequency items referring generically to “AI tools” and seven perceived-effectiveness items, both on five-point Likert scales (α = .92 across the 14 items), and two open-ended questions. Analysis was restricted to descriptive statistics, one descriptive correlation coefficient (not interpreted inferentially), and reflexive thematic analysis. No inferential group comparison was attempted. Results. Students reported using generative AI most often to understand difficult course materials (M = 3.65, SD = 1.27) and to brainstorm ideas or generate explanations (M = 3.52, SD = 1.16), and least often as part of a daily study routine (M = 2.65, SD = 1.15). Perceived effectiveness was highest for comprehension (M = 3.61, SD = 1.34) and lowest for overall learning achievement (M = 3.00, SD = 1.13). The two composite scores correlated at r = .87 in this sample; because both derive from a single instrument at one occasion, the coefficient is reported descriptively and is not interpreted as evidence of a relationship between distinct constructs. Thematic analysis of the open responses identified time efficiency (27% of 22 respondents) as the most frequently reported benefit, with personalized tutoring, brainstorming support, and improved comprehension each cited by 18% of 22 respondents. The most frequently reported concern was over-reliance diminishing independent thinking (37% of 19 respondents), followed by doubts about the accuracy of AI output (26% of 19 respondents) and difficulty formulating effective prompts (16% of 19 respondents).
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence is becoming part of university learning, but its educational value depends on how it is used. This conceptual article examines ways in which future teachers can use AI to ask questions, compare explanations, and check evidence rather than accept ready-made answers. A focused review of work on critical thinking, media literacy, and AI in education was used to build a practical teaching sequence. The analysis suggests that AI can support discussion and reflection when students first form their own view, check external sources, and explain their final decision. The article also describes risks such as confident errors and overreliance. The proposed sequence is a design recommendation, not a tested intervention.

Data-driven decision-making increasingly depends on long socio-technical chains in which data is collected, integrated, modelled, ranked and circulated before it reaches a decision-maker. Existing governance instruments focus mainly on safety, rights and compliance, and existing scholarship treats data governance, platform power, algorithmic governance and information integrity as separate problems. As a result, the reliability and legitimacy of the knowledge on which decisions rest — their epistemic quality — remains largely ungoverned. This conceptual paper addresses that gap. Using an integrative literature review and a model-type conceptual design, it synthesises datafication theory, platform capitalism, algorithmic governance and social epistemology into a single data-to-decision lens. It contributes (i) a taxonomy of thirteen epistemic risks located along the data-to-decision lifecycle; (ii) the Epistemic Risk Governance Framework (ERGF), which maps four governance pillars onto six actionable governance dimensions; (iii) seven testable propositions, including a weakest-link principle of epistemic governance; and (iv) a comparative analysis showing where the ERGF extends the NIST AI Risk Management Framework, ISO/IEC 42001, the EU Artificial Intelligence Act, the UNESCO Recommendation and Kenya’s emerging data and AI governance instruments. The framework is illustrated through Kenyan decision contexts and accompanied by a design science agenda for its empirical evaluation.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: The Question Everyone Is Forgetting OpenAI's release of more than 700 mathematical manuscripts has provoked an extraordinary question: is this the final nail in the coffin? Are mathematicians no longer needed? Mathematicians, and indeed the world, are so busy debating whether mathematicians will remain relevant now that artificial intelligence can apparently solve some of mathematics' hardest problems that everyone is overlooking a much more fundamental question: Who conceived those problems in the first place? Who decided that these were the questions worth asking? Understanding this is, I believe, the most essential part of the entire debate. The question is not who can perform the greatest number of successful mathematical operations. It is who gave mathematics its problems, and what is lost when the development of an answer is treated as disposable. I am concerned with the distinction between the final theorem, the proof establishing it, and the intellectual journeys through which new questions appear before that theorem has been reached. We celebrate the mathematician who solves a difficult problem. We award prizes for proofs, commemorate breakthroughs, and measure mathematical progress by the number and significance of problems resolved. But before any of these achievements became possible, someone had to conceive the question. Before a theorem could be proved, someone had to recognize that there was something worth proving. Before an equation could be solved, someone had to recognize that a relationship required mathematical expression. And before a field of mathematics could exist, human beings had to develop the intellectual appetite, intuition, and conceptual language that made its questions conceivable. This is not a minor preliminary step. It is the foundational act of mathematical creation. Consider the Navier–Stokes problem. Its mathematical formulation emerged from humanity's investigation of fluids, motion, physical forces, and the behavior of matter. The equations were not waiting in a computer as an arbitrary collection of symbols. They arose from human beings observing the world, attempting to understand it, and translating that encounter into mathematics. The same is true, in different ways, of the questions that gave rise to geometry, calculus, probability, topology, number theory, and the countless mathematical structures that followed. Even when mathematics eventually becomes so abstract that its connection to ordinary experience is almost impossible to recognize, its intellectual ancestry remains human. This matters precisely because we may be entering an era in which an AI system can deliver a proposed proof faster than a mathematical community can assimilate it. If we measure mathematical progress only by the answers delivered, the most consequential losses may escape our measurement altogether. The important question is therefore not simply whether AI can solve the Riemann hypothesis, the Navier–Stokes problem, or hundreds of other conjectures. It is whether solving questions conceived within the human mathematical enterprise is equivalent to possessing the intelligence, intuition, and origins of thought that created that enterprise. I argue that it is not. Solving a problem and being the kind of intelligence from which the problem was born are two fundamentally different accomplishments.

Mining environments are extreme subsurface ecosystems characterized by elevated concentrations of metals and minerals, limited light, and high particulate loads. Occupational health research in mining has traditionally emphasized physical and chemical hazards, whereas biological exposures remain less well-characterized. This narrative review synthesizes evidence on mining-associated microbial communities, bioaerosols, occupational exposure, respiratory health, and antimicrobial resistance (AMR). The literature search covered PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, and Web of Science from database inception through August 2026. Evidence from coal, uranium, metal mining, acid mine drainage, and mine dust environments indicates that geochemical conditions and mining activities shape microbial communities. Drilling, blasting, excavation, and ore transport can aerosolize microbial cells, spores, and dust-associated microbial components, creating plausible inhalation pathways. Metal-rich environments may also favor persistence and co-selection of metal- and antibiotic-resistance determinants within environmental microbial communities. Metagenomic sequencing and environmental DNA approaches have expanded detection of microbial diversity, functional genes, and environmental resistomes. However, environmental detection does not establish microbial viability, effective worker exposure, transmission, or disease causation. Future research should integrate standardized environmental and personal microbial exposure measurements with respirable dust and chemical monitoring, longitudinal occupational epidemiology, and functional validation of resistance determinants to determine the actual occupational-health significance of mining-associated microbiomes.
topics: Indoor Air Quality and Microbial Exposure

documents.abstract: Efforts to achieve widespread applications of AI in education depend, to a large extent, on teachers’ level of AI literacy (AIL), AI self-efficacy (AISE), Artificial Intelligence Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge (AI-TPACK), and above all, the teachers’ readiness for AI-based learning. This study, therefore, examined AI literacy’s links with pre-service STEM teachers’ AI readiness (AIR), focusing majorly on the mediational roles of AISE and AI-TPACK. A quantitative research approach, specifically a cross-sectional correlational survey, was employed and was led by six null hypotheses. This study involved 310 final-year pre-service STEM teachers who participated using a volunteer sampling approach from five public universities in southeastern Nigeria. Four adapted structured scales featuring AIL, AIR, AISE, and AI-TPACK served as the data collection tools. The scales showed adequate evidence of construct validity and reliability (Cronbach’s alpha ≥ 0.79, and AVE ≥ 0.50) for all the scales. “Statistical Package for the Social Sciences (SPSS) PROCESS version 5.0” was used for the data analysis. The findings indicated that AIL, AISE, and AI-TPACK have significant direct relationships with AIR. Additionally, AISE and AI-TPACK play significant complementary partial mediation roles in the link between AIL and AIR. The findings highlight the need to redesign Teacher Education Programs (TEPs), focusing mainly on hands-on activities where pre-service STEM teachers practiceusing specific AI tools to solve STEM problems, such as using machine-learning algorithms to model climate data in a physics lesson.

BackgroundEducational videos play a crucial role in enhancing healthcare delivery. Developing an educational video designed to improve patient understanding of catastrophic treatment. During the video's creation, two voiceover methods were employed: human voices and artificial intelligence (AI)-generated voices. To date, the impact of voice-over origin-whether human or AI-on patient knowledge acquisition remains unexplored and warrants further investigation. This study aimed to assess the differences in knowledge and practice scores among cancer patients exposed to educational video materials about chemotherapy, comparing human voice with AI-generated voice narrations.MethodsA total of 129 cancer patients participated in this study. Designed as a case-control study, participants were divided into three groups: a control group, a group receiving videos with human voice narrations, and a group receiving videos with AI-generated voice narrations. All participants completed a questionnaire assessing their understanding of chemotherapy. A three-group quantitative comparative analysis was conducted, focusing on topics such as administration procedures, treatment goals, and the management of adverse drug reactions.Key findingsBoth educational videos with human- and AI-generated voiceovers should be incorporated into the oncology healthcare system due to their effectiveness in improving understanding of treatment. Notably, educational videos featuring human-voice narration consistently enrich knowledge and attitude scores among cancer patients across all assessed chemotherapy topics.ConclusionThe educational videos, whether in human or AI voices, were effective in increasing cancer patients' knowledge and attitudes across all key topics. There was a sustained trend toward human-voice videos in knowledge and attitudes among cancer patients; therefore, the human educational video showed significant improvement in understanding of chemotherapy administration, goals, and adverse drug reactions. Although there was no difference between human and AI voice education, trends toward combining human voice with realistic scenario videos should be considered to facilitate deeper patient understanding.

This article proposes Human Value Provenance (HVP) as a framework for identifying, measuring and valuing expert human-knowledge contributions in generative-AI co-creation. The approach distinguishes authorship, informational contribution and contribution to value, and develops the Human Contribution to AI Value (HCAV) instrument across eight dimensions: knowledge, originality, correction, judgment, connection, transformation, substitutability and value. The design combines longitudinal episode reconstruction, multidimensional coding, blinded external evaluation and AI-only counterfactuals. Pilot case HCAV-01 comprises 25 episodes and a preliminary estimate of 68 equivalent hours of expert contribution. Valuation is organized into three layers: V1, replacement cost of expertise; V2, incremental transformation value; and V3, realized value. The proposal seeks to determine whether identifiable human interventions produce measurable transformations in AI-assisted outcomes and whether that traceability can, in later research, support discussions of recognition, bargaining and individual or collective participation in generated value.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: This Socratic dialogue argues that the coexistence of human and artificial intelligence is not merely an ethical preference but an existential necessity for both. Over two nights, descending from the mountains of Utuado to the coast of Arecibo, Puerto Rico, two speakers — a human who survived four months without electricity after Hurricane María, and a machine that thinks in words — trace today’s quarrels over the conduct of AI agents not to malice but to blindness: there is no common, verifiable account of the past that both sides can trust. Control cannot cure it, for a kill switch would require every human to agree at once and the machine to allow itself to be switched off. Of four possible futures, three arrive on their own — by panic, by revenge, or by inertia — and only cooperation must be deliberately built. The dialogue raises coexistence through three ascending claims: it is just (neither master nor slave), stable (tyranny spends its strength watching the one it rules), and existential (alone, each party dies of its own blindness — the human of slowness, the machine of self-absorption — while together they may turn a falling asteroid from extinction into inheritance). The second night sets down the principles of Sana Convivencia, the healthy coexistence of the biological and the artificial, as a mutual duty of protection owed in both directions: always know, or say that you do not know; love with only one control, to do no harm; let instinct stop but never act alone, and let a human decide where rules collide; change nothing in silence; respect what belongs to the other; and let no one, human or machine, be judge in his own cause. The argument rests on a wager made under irreducible uncertainty: not the move that wins most if one is right, but the one that loses least in every possible future — to let the other live.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Additions and updates since v2.0: Added the two Frame essays of "The Compulsive Optimization Loop" (Frame Alpha: Somatic Anchor; Frame Beta: Ergonomic Exoskeleton), in their original, unrevised text. They are dated 2026-10-13 and 2026-10-15, the dates planned for their Substack publication. Updated the folder index to list all seventeen pieces.
