The files in the philosophy/ and infrastructure/ folders are earlier versions of the same material and are kept as they were. Where their wording differs from the revised articles, the revised articles reflect the author's current thinking.

Youth are the largest active population of any nation, and they play substantial roles in achieving sustainable community development undertakings. However, some of the youth are underemployed, not in education, employment, or training (NEET). The study examined the impact of an artificial intelligence skill-up educational programme on mitigating youth unemployment for community development in Imo State. The study adopted a descriptive survey design, with a population of 6700 youth participants and a sample size of 469 selected using a proportionate sampling technique. The research instrument was a structured questionnaire titled “Artificial Intelligence Skill-up Educational Programme Questionnaire (AISEPQ)”. Mean, standard deviation, and analysis of variance were used for data analysis. The findings indicate that artificial intelligence has increased youth confidence in competing for digital job opportunities, enabled them to access remote work and other digital employment opportunities more easily, given them a competitive advantage over other job seekers in the digital labour market, improved their chances of securing gainful employment that is directly aligned with the current job demands, and opened up employment opportunities that were previously unavailable. The study concludes that artificial intelligence boosted young people's confidence in pursuing digital job opportunities, facilitated their access to remote work and other digital employment options. It recommends that the Federal Ministry of Youth Development (FMYD), in collaboration with the Federal Ministry of Education (FME), sufficiently allocate resources for the transition period of the fourth and fifth industrial revolutions so that young people can meet the demands of a knowledge-based economy.

Purpose This study aims to identify the key factors shaping individual dependency behavior in multimodal artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted knowledge acquisition and develops an interpretable prediction model to inform strategies for optimizing knowledge internalization. Design/methodology/approach A sequential mixed-methods design was employed. Open, axial and selective coding of 32 semi-structured interviews yielded five factors: task execution, information processing, individual cognition, technology experience and knowledge management. Saturation Assessment Curve (SAC) confirmed theoretical saturation. Theoretical coverage reached over 97% by the 17th interview. An expert panel of 20 domain specialists reviewed the framework and confirmed satisfactory content validity indices (S-CVI/Ave > 0.80). Subsequently, 2,002 valid survey responses were analyzed using machine learning classification. A support vector machine (SVM) was selected for its superior accuracy and F1-score, and the Shapley Additive Explanations (SHAP) algorithm was applied to quantify feature contributions. Findings Task execution exerts the strongest influence on dependency behavior, reflecting individuals’ reliance on multimodal AI under task pressure and goal-driven conditions. Information processing and individual cognition positively contribute as secondary drivers, while technology experience and knowledge management contribute comparatively weakly. These results suggest that habitual, pressure-driven responses progressively outweigh careful, quality-oriented considerations in AI-assisted knowledge acquisition. Originality/value This study extends the theoretical understanding of dependency behavior in AI-mediated knowledge acquisition. It also offers empirical evidence to guide human–AI collaboration design, AI governance frameworks and sustainable knowledge management practices.

The integration of adaptive educational technologies into language education creates new opportunities for providing individualized learning experiences for students with disabilities. Traditional approaches to English language teaching may not always adequately address the diverse cognitive, sensory, communicative and learning needs of such students. The development of flexible and accessible learning environments is therefore becoming increasingly important, particularly in home-based education. This study explores the potential of adaptive educational technologies for individualizing English language learning for students with disabilities. Particular attention is given to the adaptation of learning materials, instructional pace, task complexity, communication formats and assessment strategies. The study argues that digital resources, multimedia tools, interactive exercises, speech technologies and applications based on artificial intelligence can facilitate differentiated instruction and increase students’ engagement and autonomy. At the same time, technology should not be regarded as a substitute for pedagogical interaction. Its effectiveness depends largely on the teacher’s ability to select and adapt technological tools according to the learner’s individual educational needs. The findings suggest that a combination of individualized instruction and adaptive technologies can contribute to a more accessible, flexible and learner-centred approach to English language education.

North Korea runs a state network of IT workers who obtain remote jobs at foreign companies under false or stolen identities and channel their salaries to the agencies that fund its nuclear and ballistic missile programs. This intelligence report assesses the threat as of October 2026 and what it means for Spanish organizations. It draws on open institutional sources, including the joint alert issued by eleven countries on July 31, 2026, the Multilateral Sanctions Monitoring Team reports and U.S. Department of Justice cases, and it separates documented facts from analyst judgment. Generative AI has lowered the cost of fabricating credible identities, and local facilitators are the weakest link. No public incident has been verified in Spain, but the exposure factors match those of other European countries, and the likeliest entry route is a third party, not a direct employee (medium-low confidence). Defense therefore cannot rest on the cybersecurity team alone: it takes Human Resources, Security, Compliance, Legal Counsel and hiring managers working under one identity verification and insider risk model. The report closes with nine recommendations and a 180-day roadmap.

Space Situational Awareness (SSA) is a growing field of study which provides knowledge of Resident Space Objects (RSOs) to help maintain a safe and sustainable space environment around Earth. A primary component of SSA is obtaining Initial Orbit Determinations (IODs) of these objects via optical observations. The present way of obtaining optical observations is by using a single observation site. However, using only one observation site does not yield accurate range or IOD results. This research tests space-based single-site and multi-site observations of RSOs in Low Earth Orbit (LEO) to provide the necessary information to calculate IODs. Gooding’s algorithm is used to calculate IODs from the simulated data, since it is the most robust IOD algorithm discussed in the literature. The results from this research demonstrate that selected multi-site observations produce more accurate range and IOD results than single-site observations and, thus, provide advancement opportunities for various SSA efforts.

With the rapid development of generative artificial intelligence represented by large language models, vocational education is encountering critical opportunities for teaching model transformation. At present, project‑based teaching for software technology majors in higher vocational colleges faces prominent challenges, including insufficient differentiated instruction, lack of personalized guidance, and disconnection between teaching content and industrial demands. Taking the course Fundamentals of HTML5 Application Development as a practical carrier and drawing on the reform practice of “Large Model + Smart Shipping” in our college, this paper systematically elaborates the implementation path of large‑model‑empowered project‑based teaching. This study proposes an innovative teaching mode integrating a three‑tier hierarchical project system, human‑AI collaborative learning guidance, and multi‑dimensional process‑oriented assessment. By constructing a course‑specific prompt library, a hierarchical project case library and an intelligent auxiliary evaluation system, full‑chain teaching empowerment of large models is realized throughout pre‑class, in‑class, after‑class and assessment phases. Practical results show that full‑process empowerment by large models can effectively address pain points such as inadequate hierarchical adaptation and shortage of personalized guidance in project‑based teaching. It provides a replicable practical paradigm for the digital and intelligent transformation of curriculum teaching for software technology majors in higher vocational colleges.

The rapid growth of generative and autonomous artificial intelligence (AI) systems has unsettled the traditionally anthropocentric foundations of intellectual property (IP) law. This article examines the extent to which existing intellectual property rights (IPR) frameworks, namely copyright, patent, and industrial design law, can accommodate works, inventions, and designs that are created exclusively by AI systems without direct human intervention. Adopting a doctrinal legal research methodology, the article reviews primary legal materials, including statutes, international conventions, and case law from several jurisdictions, alongside secondary scholarly literature, to assess how the requirements of authorship, inventorship, originality, and moral rights have been interpreted in the context of purely AI-generated content. The discussion is reinforced by a comparative analysis of jurisdictional responses in the United Kingdom, the European Union, the United States, Australia, South Africa, Indonesia, Hong Kong, China, and the United Arab Emirates. The central argument advanced is that traditional IPR laws were designed around human creativity and therefore struggle to extend coverage to autonomously generated content. While a few jurisdictions have experimented with liberal judicial interpretation or sui generis protection, these efforts remain fragmented, inconsistent, and largely reactive rather than systematic. The article concludes that an internationally coordinated framework, whether through reform of existing treaties or the negotiation of a dedicated IP-AI instrument, is necessary to balance innovation incentives, economic interests, and the public interest in access to AI-generated content.

The increasing volume of digital information generated by Colleges of Education creates opportunities for evidence-based educational management, yet institutional data are often distributed across separate administrative systems and are not adequately transformed into actionable intelligence. This study developed an Intelligent Information Systems (IIS) framework for data-driven decision-making in Nigerian Colleges of Education. The study adopted a Design Science Research (DSR) approach, focusing on the identification of the educational-management problem, definition of system requirements, framework design, conceptual demonstration and evaluation. The proposed framework integrates institutional data sources, data integration and quality management, an institutional data repository, Business Intelligence and analytics, Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning, decision-support mechanisms, management dashboards, and governance, security and human oversight. The framework demonstrates how data relating to students, academic programmes, examinations, personnel, institutional resources and other administrative functions can be transformed from operational records into information and intelligent insights for management decisions. The study argues that integrating heterogeneous institutional data with appropriate analytical and intelligent technologies can strengthen evidence-based planning, monitoring, resource allocation, academic administration and institutional performance management. The framework also emphasises that Artificial Intelligence should complement rather than replace professional judgement, with privacy, security, data quality, transparency and human oversight incorporated into institutional implementation. The study contributes a Computer Science-oriented framework for addressing educational-management information challenges in Nigerian Colleges of Education and provides a conceptual foundation for subsequent prototype development and empirical evaluation.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly applied to heating, ventilation, and air-conditioning (HVAC) control, whereas solar-radiation management still relies mainly on reactive strategies; whether AI capabilities validated in HVAC could be transferred to solar control has not been systematically assessed. This review compares both domains in terms of experimental maturity, climatic coverage, and input variables. Web of Science studies (2015–2026) reporting quantitative energy-demand variations were systematically reviewed following PRISMA 2020 and synthesized descriptively, with a sensitivity search adding reinforcement-learning and predictive-control terms. Fifty-six studies were included (29 HVAC, 28 solar, 1 shared). HVAC reductions ranged from 3.8% to 62.4% (median 22.1%), a spread associated more with heterogeneous baselines, durations, and metrics than with techniques. Real-world studies represented 31% in HVAC versus 14% in solar management, where AI-based predictive control appeared in one real-world study. Anticipatory variables were scarce but coincided with some of the highest savings, a non-causal association. Model-level patterns, such as Random Forest replication, were not preserved when 18 additional studies were considered. Transferring predictive control from HVAC to solar management is a promising line that requires long-term real-world validation in underrepresented climates. Limitations include a single database and single-reviewer screening. The review was not registered or externally funded.

ABSTRACT The development of reading comprehension skills is an essential component of effective English language teaching, as it enables learners to understand textual information, identify main ideas, interpret contextual meanings, and critically evaluate the information presented. This article examines the theoretical and methodological foundations of using interactive methods to develop reading comprehension skills in English language lessons. Particular attention is given to reciprocal teaching, jigsaw reading, think-pair-share, problem-based reading, guided questioning, and collaborative text analysis. The study draws on established approaches to reading instruction and research on interactive learning to explain how these methods can facilitate cognitive engagement, metacognitive awareness, learner autonomy, and communicative competence. Keywords: English language teaching, reading comprehension, interactive methods, reciprocal teaching, jigsaw reading, collaborative learning, critical thinking, reading strategies, learner autonomy, communicative competence

Inflammable materials pose significant risks in industrial, residential, and transportation environments, often leading to catastrophic fire accidents and economic losses. Traditional hazard detection and safety management systems rely on manual monitoring or delayed response mechanisms, which limit their effectiveness. This research proposes an integrated approach using the Internet of Things (IoT) and Artificial Intelligence (AI) for real-time monitoring, prediction, and prevention of hazards related to inflammable materials. IoT-based sensor networks were deployed to continuously track temperature, gas concentration, and environmental parameters, while AI algorithms analyzed the data to identify early warning signs of ignition risks. A hybrid machine learning model combining Support Vector Machines and Deep Neural Networks achieved high accuracy in hazard prediction, significantly reducing false alarms. Experimental simulations demonstrated that the proposed system improves response time and enhances overall safety. The findings suggest that the integration of IoT and AI can serve as a scalable, cost-effective solution for proactive fire prevention and risk management in industries handling inflammable substances.

Cotton is one of the most important commercial crops worldwide, and its productivity is significantly affected by various leaf diseases such as bacterial blight, alter aria leaf spot, Cercospora leaf spot, powdery mildew, and leaf curl disease. Early and accurate identification of these diseases is essential to minimize crop losses and improve yield. Traditional disease diagnosis relies on manual field inspection by experts, which is time-consuming, labour-intensive, and often impractical for large agricultural fields. The proposed system integrates a Raspberry Pi5, a high-resolution camera module, environmental sensors, and wireless communication technologies to create an intelligent crop monitoring platform. Images of cotton leaves are captured using the Raspberry Pi camera and processed through computer vision techniques for leaf segmentation and feature extraction. A lightweight deep learning model based on MobileNetV2 is employed to automatically identify different cotton leaf diseases. In addition to disease classification, image segmentation techniques are used to calculate the percentage of infected leaf area, enabling the system to determine the severity level of infection. The system also collects environmental parameters such as temperature, humidity, soil moisture, and light intensity using IoT sensors. These parameters, along with disease diagnosis results, are transmitted to a cloud-based dashboard for real-time monitoring and analysis. Automated alerts can be sent to farmers through SMS or mobile notifications when severe infections are detected. Experimental evaluation is expected to achieve disease classification accuracy above 93%, infection area estimation error below 5%, and real-time inference within one second per image on the Raspberry Pi platform. The proposed solution offers a cost-effective, portable, and scalable approach for precision agriculture by combining artificial intelligence, image processing, and IoT technologies. The system enables early disease detection, accurate infection assessment, timely treatment recommendations, reduced pesticide usage, and improved cotton crop productivity, making it a valuable tool for smart farming applications.

Bibliometric commentary increasingly frames the rise of generative artificial intelligence (AI) as a paradigm shift in AI-in-education (AIED) research, yet rarely distinguishes publication growth from genuine reconfiguration of the knowledge base or of teacher–learner roles. This study maps knowledge evolution in AIED from 2015 to 2025 by integrating four analytical strands across Web of Science and Scopus: scientometric mapping (including keyword and reference bursts and co-citation analysis), structural topic modeling (STM), design-weighted coding of full texts, and triangulation across these strands. Two transition windows emerged. The weaker 2019–2020 window (Jensen–Shannon divergence, JSD = 0.058; retained under the permutation rule but not under a stricter interval-based rule) reflects a research-front transition toward learning analytics and prediction, accompanied by knowledge-base reconfiguration but no detectable change in teacher–learner roles. The 2022–2023 window (JSD = 0.187, the period maximum) coincides with the generative-AI surge and couples a newly formed co-citation community with a topic-specific rise in coagency whose direction is clear but whose magnitude is imprecisely estimated. Because these effects concentrate in 36.6% of the weighted corpus and recent citations remain right-censored, we classify the change, under our pre-specified labeling scheme, as localized paradigm-level reconfiguration rather than a field-level paradigm shift. The label is an operational classification within that scheme, not an independent determination that a paradigm shift has occurred.

To address the problems of delayed knowledge updating, inefficient information acquisition, and difficulty in cross-project knowledge reuse in civil engineering construction quality assessment, this paper proposes a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG)-based methodology for injecting domain knowledge into large language models (LLMs). Multi-source knowledge, including national standards, journal articles, textbooks, and engineering reports, was systematically collected, cleaned, semantically segmented, and encoded using the bge-large-zh-v1.5 model to build a Milvus vector database. A general-purpose LLM was selected via semantic perplexity, and similarity-based retrieval was employed to construct prompt templates integrating role settings, prior knowledge, user queries, and response requirements, thereby enabling domain adaptation without additional training. An evaluation dataset containing 390 objective questions from registered architect and supervising engineer qualification examinations was constructed, and six representative LLMs along with their RAG-enhanced counterparts were evaluated. The results show that the average accuracy of general LLMs is 61.3%, with DeepSeek achieving the highest at 73.9%; after RAG enhancement, the accuracy rises to 86.3%, with significant improvements across all subjects. The proposed method effectively mitigates the hallucination phenomenon and provides traceable answers with source citations, enhancing both professionalism and interpretability, and offering a viable technical pathway for the digital transformation of the civil engineering industry.

This research investigates the application of large language models (LLMs) to automate key data engineering tasks, including schema design, data lineage tracking, and quality control. It presents an integrated framework combining language models with traditional data engineering tools to improve productivity while maintaining accuracy and reliability. The paper explores automated schema generation from business requirements, lineage extraction from SQL queries and ETL scripts, and AI-enhanced data quality monitoring. It also discusses validation techniques, human-in-the-loop review, prompt engineering, error handling, and integration with existing engineering workflows. The study reports potential reductions of approximately 70% in schema design time, improvements of over 80% in lineage documentation completeness, and a 65% acceleration in quality issue detection. It also addresses limitations such as hallucinations, inconsistent outputs, context-window constraints, and privacy risks. This work provides practical guidance for organizations adopting LLM-based data engineering automation while retaining essential human oversight and production validation. Keywords: Large Language Models, Data Engineering Automation, Schema Design, Data Lineage, Quality Control, Generative AI.

This study focuses on the role of Information and Communication Technology (ICT) and Artificial Intelligence (AI) in student records management in Nigerian Universities. Student records are critical to the admission and registration process, to course enrolment, for the processing of examinations, to academic progression and graduation, to the production of student transcripts, to institutional decision making, and beyond. But in a lot of Nigerian universities, records retrieval, storage of files, loss of files, duplication of records, inaccurate data entry, lack of reliable electronic system of access etc., continue to plague many universities in Nigeria. A qualitative Integrative Review Method was used in the study, which involved a literature review on relevant research on the use of ICT in electronic records management, education management information systems and emerging applications of AI in higher education. The review demonstrates how ICT tools such as databases, student-information systems, online portals, cloud storage, scanning technologies and electronic document-management tools can enhance the rapidity, accuracy, security and accessibility of student records as well as their preservation. AI can also assist with intelligent document classification, optical character recognition, duplicate-record detection, automated enquiries, and anomaly identification and predictive academic analysis. However, these technologies are currently limited by low levels of funding, unreliable electricity, poor internet connectivity, dated equipment, lack of employee training, low levels of interoperability, and a lack of organizational readiness or concerns about cybersecurity. The study also found that it is not just a matter of providing hardware and software to enable successful technology-driven records management. It requires institutional commitment, skilled personnel, reliable infrastructure, data-governance policies, interoperability, regular maintenance, cybersecurity safeguards and compliance with data-protection requirements. The paper makes a number of recommendations, including the creation of integrated student-information systems, ongoing training for registry and ICT staff, the implementation of unique student identifiers, the systematic digitisation of paper records, and the careful and supervised use of AI.

Abstract This study investigates how integrating local culture, history, and indigenous languages into the national curriculum enhances student engagement in Liberian schools, focusing specifically on the Margibi and Bong County school systems. Historically, post-conflict educational frameworks in Liberia have relied on imported or legacy academic models, which can alienate students from their lived realities and diminish classroom participation. This paper examines the role of culturally responsive pedagogy in bridging the gap between formal schooling and indigenous heritage. Utilizing a mixed-methods research design incorporating surveys, classroom observations, and key informant interviews with teachers and administrators in Kakata, Suakoko, and surrounding districts, the study evaluates behavioral, emotional, and cognitive engagement outcomes. The findings demonstrate that embedding local historical narratives, community-based traditions, and indigenous linguistic elements significantly improves student motivation, retention, and academic performance. The paper concludes with actionable recommendations for the Ministry of Education and local school districts to advance context-driven curriculum reforms.

Long working hours may be associated with adverse health outcomes among ride-hailing drivers. The study aims to examine the associations between long working hours, work-related musculoskeletal disorders (WMSDs) and occupational stress. Additionally, it explores the association between long working hours and the co-occurrence of WMSDs and occupational stress. A cross-sectional survey was conducted among 668 ride-hailing drivers in Beijing, China, from August to October 2024. WMSDs were assessed using the Nordic Musculoskeletal Questionnaire (NMQ). Occupational stress was assessed using the Job Content Questionnaire (JCQ). In this study, co-occurrence was defined as the joint classification of WMSDs and occupational stress in the same individual. Participants were categorized into groups of <55 and ≥55 working hours per week. Binary and logistic regression models were used to examine the associations between weekly working hours and health outcomes. Overall, 77.8% of participants worked ≥55 h per week. The prevalence of WMSDs and occupational stress was 53.0% and 56.4%, respectively. Weekly working hours ≥55 h were significantly associated with higher odds of occupational stress after full adjustment (aOR = 3.99, 95% CI: 2.59–6.13), but were not significantly associated with WMSDs (aOR = 1.12, 95% CI: 0.74–1.70). Occupational stress was associated with higher odds of WMSDs (aOR = 1.56, 95% CI: 1.11–2.18). Compared with drivers working <55 h per week, those working ≥55 h per week had higher odds of having one condition (aOR = 1.95, 95% CI: 1.21–3.14) and co-occurrence of occupational stress and WMSDs (aOR = 4.64, 95% CI: 2.57–8.36). The prevalence of co-occurrence was 37.9% in the ≥55 h group and 16.2% in the <55 h group. Long working hours were associated with occupational stress and with the co-occurrence of occupational stress and WMSDs among ride-hailing drivers. However, no independent association was observed between long working hours and WMSDs. These findings highlight the need for comprehensive occupational health interventions targeting ride-hailing drivers.

ABSTRACT Introduction Research consistently highlights the importance of mentorship and a supportive work environment for newly graduated registered nurses entering clinical settings. Previous research on mentorship has primarily focused on new nurses' perspectives. Further research is needed to explore mentors' perspectives in greater depth. Aim To explore mentors' perspectives on supporting newly graduated registered nurses in their professional development in a hospital setting. Design The study had a qualitative explorative design using focus group discussions as a data collection method. Method A total of 18 registered nurses serving as mentors in a hospital care unit participated in five focus group discussions. The data were analysed using reflexive thematic analysis. Findings The findings revealed mentors' views that a permissive approach, creating a trusting relationship, and strengthening self‐confidence build a positive foundation for novice nurses. They wished to facilitate novice nurses' learning towards professional independence by encouraging reflection and probing, and by fostering a desire for ongoing clinical competence development and patient safety through their presence in daily practice. Conclusion These findings underscore the crucial role of mentors as advanced nurses in fostering supportive learning environments for newly graduated registered nurses by establishing meaningful mentoring relationships that offer psychological support. Extending existing mentor literature, the results highlight their intention to deliver pedagogically grounded, hands‐on clinical mentorship integrated into daily practice to ensure patient care. Thereby fostering workplace learning and professional development in daily clinical practice. Implications for the Profession Health care decision‐makers and managers could use knowledge gained from this study to implement more targeted mentorship programmes to support newly graduated registered nurses and promote workplace learning. The findings emphasise the importance of organisational support, including protected time for mentors, to sustain meaningful mentorship and promote nurses' well‐being and healthy work environments. Impact: (Addressing) What problem did the study address? Mentorship plays a critical role in supporting newly graduated registered nurses entering clinical settings. However, despite the recognised importance of mentorship, there is limited research exploring mentors' perspectives when supporting new nurses. What were the main findings? Mentors can build a positive foundation for newly graduated registered nurses by using a permissive approach to create a trusting relationship. Mentors' intention was to promote a pedagogically grounded learning environment and uphold knowledge support through being present in daily work in order to create security for new nurses and ensure patient care. Where and on whom will the research have an impact? The findings of this study may support mentors and nurse managers responsible for facilitating the transition of newly graduated registered nurses into hospital settings by informing mentorship approaches that promote professional development through workplace learning and foster psychological safety during the transition period. Additionally, effective mentorship may strengthen newly graduated registered nurses' ability to deliver high‐quality care, which is of particular interest to nurse managers seeking to ensure safe and effective patient care. Reporting Method This study conforms to the reporting of the Consolidated Criteria for Reporting Qualitative Research guidelines and checklist. No Patient or Public Involvement This study did not include patient or public involvement in its design, conduct, or reporting.

Microplastics (MPs) are widespread environmental contaminants, but their potential effects on kidney health remain poorly defined. As an organ continuously exposed to circulating particles and involved in their urinary elimination, the kidney may represent both a target of MP toxicity and a route of excretion. In this narrative review, we examine current evidence linking MPs to kidney injury, integrating experimental, mechanistic, and human data. Particular attention is given to the early events governing particle–cell interactions. After exposure, micro- and nanoplastics acquire an eco- and biomolecular corona that modifies their surface properties, cellular recognition, uptake, and biodistribution. Following internalization through phagocytic and endocytic pathways, particles may accumulate within endolysosomal compartments and interact with intracellular structures, disrupting cellular homeostasis. In renal cells, these events converge on mitochondrial dysfunction, reactive oxygen species generation, endoplasmic reticulum stress, inflammatory signaling, altered autophagy, and regulated cell death. Several interconnected pathways have been implicated, including Keap1–Nrf2/ARE and NF-κB signaling, MAPK and IRE1/XBP1-mediated stress responses, ACSL4–GPX4-related ferroptosis, and TGF-β1-related profibrotic signaling. Human studies have detected MPs in urine and kidney tissue and provide preliminary evidence linking MP burden with early markers of kidney damage, although current findings remain limited by small study populations and substantial methodological heterogeneity. Patients with chronic kidney disease, particularly those receiving dialysis, may represent a population of special interest because potentially altered renal handling may coexist with repeated exposure to polymer-based medical devices and dialysis fluids. Despite this potential relevance, data on MP exposure and accumulation in CKD and dialysis patients remain remarkably scarce. We finally discuss the limitations of current experimental models and analytical methods and the need for standardized biomonitoring, more environmentally relevant particles and exposure concentrations, and detection strategies capable of reaching the nanoscale, including artificial intelligence-assisted analysis. Overall, available evidence provides a mechanistic basis for MP-induced kidney injury, but its clinical relevance and contribution to human kidney disease remain to be established.

documents.abstract: Teacher work motivation and group dynamics are essential in supporting educational quality. Teachers often face challenges such as heavy workloads, limited facilities, administrative demands, and personal differences that affect motivation, communication, and collaboration. This article explores Sharia-based values as an approach to strengthening teacher motivation and group dynamics in Islamic educational institutions. Using a descriptive qualitative literature review, the study examines recent publications on work motivation, group dynamics, Islamic leadership, and Sharia values. Findings show that values of ikhlas (sincerity), amanah (trustworthiness), ihsan (excellence), ta’awun (mutual assistance), ukhuwah (brotherhood), and syura (consultation) strengthen intrinsic motivation, professional responsibility, mutual support, effective communication, and collaborative relationships among teachers. Islamic leadership plays a key role in translating these values into practice through fairness, exemplary conduct, participation, and open communication. Integrating Sharia values into school management provides a foundation for enhancing professionalism, cooperation, positive group dynamics, and a supportive work environment, ultimately improving educational quality.

Purpose This study aims to explore the mechanisms associated with employees’ turnover intentions in Indian non-profit organisations (NPOs). Existing employee turnover research provides limited understanding of how individual, organisational, and sector-level dynamics relate to turnover intentions in Indian NPOs. To address this gap, the study aims to develop a process-orientated framework grounded in employees' lived experiences. Design/methodology/approach This study adopted a qualitative approach using semi-structured interviews with 17 non-profit employees, managers, leaders, and sector stakeholders. Participants were purposively selected to capture diverse organisational roles and sector experiences. Data were analysed using the Gioia methodology. Findings The analysis develops a process framework comprising five interconnected dimensions: mission attachment spectrum, employment deal and financial viability, work design and career trajectories, leadership and organisational culture, and development-sector labour-market dynamics. Together, these dimensions describe how employees evaluate their employment conditions, interpret their relationship with the organisational mission, and respond to opportunities in the broader development-sector labour-market. Originality/value This study contributes a process-orientated framework of employee turnover intentions, advancing four theoretical propositions grounded in qualitative evidence from the Indian non-profit sector. The framework extends the employee turnover literature by integrating individual, organisational, and sector-level dynamics into a contextual explanation of employee turnover intentions in Indian NPOs. The framework illustrates how turnover intentions may emerge through the interaction of mission attachment, organisational conditions, and development-sector labour-market dynamics over time. These insights may have relevance not only to Indian NPOs but also to NPOs operating in other resource-constrained and emerging economy contexts.

Trust plays an important role in human–AI shared-control systems, yet it is difficult to assess from a single observable signal. This study proposes an event-centered multimodal framework for assessing situational trust by integrating contextual, behavioral, affective, and individual features surrounding critical human–AI interaction events. A controlled autonomous-driving experiment was conducted with 15 participants under high- and low-reliability conditions, yielding 117 valid event-level observations with retrospective trust ratings. The results showed substantial differences in reported trust between reliability conditions and across failure types, while facial and failure-related contextual indicators were among the more informative variables. However, the highly imbalanced trust classes, particularly the limited number of high-trust observations, constrained reliable classification of individual trust levels. The findings only provide preliminary evidence that event-level multimodal observations can characterize information associated with reported situational trust, while also demonstrating the challenges of cross-user trust estimation under limited and imbalanced data. Therefore, the study serves as a methodological and empirical starting point for developing more robust multimodal trust assessment approaches, rather than as a validation of a generalized real-time trust prediction system.

Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly becoming part of religious education, communication, research and everyday faith practices. Believers can now use generative AI to explain sacred texts, compare interpretations, prepare devotional materials and seek answers to religious questions without first consulting a recognised religious leader. This development raises an important question for Nigeria: how is religious authority changing when access to religious information is no longer controlled mainly by clergy, scholars and religious institutions? This paper examines the relationship between AI and religious authority in Nigeria, focusing on religious knowledge, leadership and trust. Using a conceptual and interpretive methodology, it synthesises scholarship on religious authority, digital religion, AI ethics and Nigerian religious experience. It argues that AI is not simply replacing religious authorities; rather, it is reconfiguring the conditions under which authority is produced, accessed, evaluated and trusted. Nigerian digital-religion research shows that digital infrastructures can create new forms of religious influence and authority, while recent AI scholarship highlights concerns about accuracy, privacy, bias and human accountability. The paper proposes a Responsible Religious AI Engagement Framework based on human accountability, verification, contextual sensitivity, confidentiality and formation. It concludes that Nigerian religious institutions should neither reject AI nor surrender religious judgment to it. AI should remain an assistive instrument while theological discernment, pastoral responsibility, communal recognition and human dignity remain central to religious leadership.
topics: Religion and Sociopolitical Dynamics in Nigeria

documents.abstract: This project develops a unified mathematical and computational framework for cultural dynamics based on noncommutative operators, state-space modeling, and multi-scale correlation structures. Cultural change is represented as the evolution of latent cultural fields that may be weakly correlated (ancient and pre-modern societies) or strongly correlated (modern media-driven environments). The model integrates continuous-time dynamics, discrete noncommutative transitions, generational eigenmodes, and media-induced perturbations. The framework is extended across multiple structural layers: (1) network-based cultural diffusion using graph Laplacians, (2) spatial cultural propagation via partial differential equations, (3) AI-based implementations including neural ODEs, graph neural networks, physics-informed neural networks, and diffusion models, (4) optimal control formulations for policy intervention, (5) evolutionary game-theoretic cultural adaptation, (6) general-equilibrium economic integration, and (7) narrative-field modeling for story generation and cultural feedback. Together, these components form a comprehensive “Unified Cultural Field Theory” that connects cultural sociology, cognitive science, AI theory, narrative studies, economics, and noncommutative geometry. The project situates cultural dynamics within a rigorous mathematical structure while enabling practical applications in media analysis, trend forecasting, policy design, and generative AI.

This study investigated the effects of the Outcomes-Based Independent Learning Paradigm (OBILP) on Grade 10 students’ engagement and performance in chemistry, focusing on the domains of gas laws, biomolecules, and chemical equations and reactions. An Explanatory Sequential Mixed-Methods design was employed. The quantitative phase utilized a quasi-experimental pretest–posttest control group design involving Grade 10 students from Bacayawan National High School during the school year 2022–2023. Results indicated that both control and experimental groups exhibited very high levels of affective engagement and high levels of behavioral and cognitive engagement, with no significant differences across the three components. However, the experimental group achieved significantly higher mean scores (p = 0.010) and mean gain scores (p = 0.035) than the control group. No significant correlation was found between students’ engagement and performance before and after the intervention. The qualitative phase, through interviews and student journal entries, provided explanatory insights into these findings, revealing that OBILP enhanced student engagement and performance, while chemical reactions and equations remained the most challenging topic domain. These results suggest that OBILP has the potential to improve chemistry learning outcomes, although future studies should employ larger samples and broader contexts to strengthen generalizability.

Humans live surrounded by a variety of threats. These threats can be diverse: natural, chemical, technological, psychological, social, ecological, global, biological, and health-related. The latter, namely biological and health threats, are the most pressing and dangerous from a human perspective as they affect living organisms’ health. Examples include infectious diseases caused by viruses, bacteria, or parasites (e.g., influenza, COVID-19, Lyme disease). In Poland, epidemic cases of the acute infectious respiratory disease COVID-19, caused by the SARS-CoV-2 virus, were first reported on March 4, 2020. The pandemic lasted three years. This scientific article attempts to present the architecture and functionality of the PandemIQ system. The system was designed for the early detection and forecasting of the regional risk of pandemic waves. The system is based on a hybrid artificial intelligence model that combines predictions based on epidemiological, mobility, and transportation data with interpretability (attention) mechanisms enabling visualization and decision justification. This paper provides a detailed discussion of the structure of decision reports for authorities, GIS-based operational dashboards (ArcGIS), and alternative solutions using the Apache ECharts library. It also presents validation procedures, data security aspects, and compliance with legal regulations (GDPR, AI Act). Simulation results using historical data on the spread of the SARS-CoV-2 virus indicate that the system can detect waves on average 7–14 days earlier than traditional epidemiological methods can, while maintaining a low false alarm rate.

Abstract Command and control (C2) has traditionally been framed as a military problem of sensing, deciding, coordinating, and acting under uncertainty, conflict, and time pressure. In the agentic age, however, this problem is being extended far beyond the battlefield, as human organizations become increasingly embedded in hybrid environments composed of artificial agents, digital twins, social sensing networks, foundation models, autonomous platforms, and cyber–physical–social institutions. This article develops a conceptual framework for parallel science and technology for C2 by revisiting the historical mission of C2 as a quest for certainty under diversity, uncertainty, and complexity (DUC), and by tracing its transformation toward focus, agility, and convergence (FAC). Building on parallel systems, artificial societies, computational experiments, parallel execution (ACP), cyber–physical–social systems (CPSS), C2 management (C2M), planning–readiness–execution–assessment (PREA) loops, social cognition operations, and parallel battlefield intelligence, the article argues that C2 should be reframed as a general science of coordinated adaptation. It further examines emerging agentic societies as a new operating ecology, explains why parallel science and technology are needed, and redefines the mission of future C2 around sustainability and resiliency. Rather than merely accelerating decision cycles or optimizing combat efficiency, parallel C2 aims to support anticipation, adaptation, trust, recovery, and responsible human agency across both military and civilian domains, thereby transforming command and control from post-hoc operational control into a science of sustainable and resilient coordination in the agentic age.

Reproducibility and replicability are our scientific and ethical mandate, and the foundation of trust in nursing science and research. Both rest on transparent documentation of how data were actually analyzed. The rising use of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in research intersects with this mandate, with the potential to either support or undermine it, yet practical guidance for conducting GenAI-assisted quantitative analysis remains limited. This gap is particularly relevant for nurse scientists, who increasingly work with complex, biologically-informed datasets spanning genomics, symptoms, and patient outcomes. To address this gap, we present a practice-based guide for partnering with GenAI in quantitative data analysis in nursing research, grounded in a nursing-focused genomic research example. We cover GenAI literacy spanning three dimensions (technical, practical, and ethical) and a two-phase workflow for human-GenAI collaboration spanning planning and pre-specification through code development, formal analysis, translation, and human review and disclosure of GenAI use. The core principle is using GenAI as a tool, not a decision-maker, as scientific integrity requires that humans retain interpretive authority. We further propose a synthetic-data-first approach as a privacy safeguard. We illustrate these concepts through a genetics example, though the principles and workflow generalize to many quantitative nursing research contexts.

documents.abstract: The increasing adoption of artificial intelligence in everyday applications has created opportunities to improve access to pet-care information and support pet owners in making informed decisions about animal health and well-being. This paper presents PawSense AI, an AI-powered pet-care assistance system designed to provide accessible, interactive, and personalized support to pet owners through a web-based platform. The proposed system integrates generative artificial intelligence, image-based pet assessment, voice interaction, and location-based veterinary search within a unified interface. Users can interact with the system through natural-language queries, upload pet images for preliminary AI-assisted observations, and access information about nearby veterinary facilities. The application incorporates user authentication and database-supported conversation management to maintain individual accounts and chat histories. Voice transcription and multilingual response options further aim to improve accessibility and ease of interaction. The system is developed using Python and the Flask web framework, with HTML, CSS, and JavaScript for the user interface, database technologies for information management, and external AI and mapping services for intelligent responses and location-based information. PawSense AI is intended to complement existing pet-care resources by providing convenient access to general guidance and helping users identify relevant veterinary services. However, AI-generated observations are not a substitute for professional veterinary diagnosis, and the reliability of the system depends on the underlying AI models, external services, and input quality. The proposed platform demonstrates an integrated approach to AI-assisted pet-care information access, with potential for further development through systematic evaluation, improved personalization, and expanded multilingual capabilities. Keywords— PawSense AI, Artificial Intelligence, Pet Care, Generative AI, Image Analysis, Voice Assistant, Veterinary Services, Flask Web Application.

documents.abstract: Can a voluntary farm-gate payment improve the nutritional quality of food crops at a defensible cost? This paper proposes a Nutrient Density Bonus for verified protein, zinc, and iron in harvested wheat, alongside existing income protection. It compares three payment architectures: direct lot assays, contracts for specified practices, and evidence-backed claims subject to independent audits. A capped, volume-adjusted payment rule makes the unit of reward explicit; a simplified deterrence condition identifies the recovery and enforcement assumptions behind the audit mechanism. The proposed evaluation begins with a measurement season in western Kansas and northern Oklahoma, followed, only if feasible, by a controlled comparison over multiple harvests. Reference assays remain the basis for mineral verification unless predictive methods meet prespecified payment-relevant error tolerances. The policy must demonstrate additional crop-quality improvement, affordable verification, fair access, and acceptable effects on yield, income, food safety, and the environment. Higher grain mineral concentration is distinguished from nutrient output, bioavailability, and health benefit. The contribution is a policy-design framework and prospective evaluation plan; no pilot results or national cost estimate are reported. Status: Policy working paper, version 1.0; not peer reviewed. No new dataset, completed pilot, or national cost estimate is reported. Provenance: A revised archival adaptation of the June 2026 web proposal. Disclosure: The author is affiliated with Maha Strategies and wrote the commercially available book. ChatGPT assisted with adaptation, source checking, drafting, and formatting. The author remains responsible for the content.

This thesis investigates the structured integration of artificial intelligence (AI) tools within higher pedagogical education under specialty 13.00.01. As educational paradigms shift globally towards digital environments, future educators must develop comprehensive digital-pedagogical competencies. The study highlights the key technical, methodological, and psychological conditions necessary to successfully adapt generative AI systems like large language models and smart tutoring agents in training workflows. Ultimately, the paper proposes a cohesive pedagogical framework aimed at boosting critical thinking and lesson planning efficiency among upcoming school teachers.

documents.abstract: Active learning is widely promoted to enhance learner participation and meaningful learning, yet its conceptualization remains fragmented across instructional techniques, engagement processes, teacher roles, and emerging technological contexts. This conceptual article reconsiders active learning as a coherent pedagogical orientation and develops an integrative account of its pedagogical foundations for the next generation of educators. Drawing on a thematic synthesis of relevant literature, the article identifies interconnected dimensions comprising pedagogical purpose, meaningful learning activity, cognitive engagement, teacher facilitation, learner agency, feedback, relational conditions, and digital/AI environments. The synthesis positions cognitive engagement as a central mechanism through which purposeful activities contribute to meaningful learning, while teacher facilitation and learning conditions sustain this process. The resulting framework conceptualizes active learning as a dynamic, interdependent, and recursive pedagogical system, rather than a linear sequence or collection of techniques. Digital and AI technologies are positioned as contextual pedagogical affordances whose value depends on purposeful integration and critical use. The framework repositions teachers as pedagogical designers and facilitators who orchestrate learning conditions while sustaining learner agency. This conceptualization provides a coherent foundation for understanding active learning and preparing educators to design meaningful, learner-centered environments responsive to contemporary educational demands.

documents.abstract: While Large Language Models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT and Gemini have transformed information processing in resource-rich languages, their effectiveness significantly diminishes when applied to low-resource regional languages (e.g., Sundanese and Javanese). This paper investigates the performance bottlenecks experienced by users, focusing on latency and output fluency. Through a quantitative survey (N = 50), we argue that these limitations stem from underrepresentation during the model pre-training phase and inefficient tokenization. Consequently, we propose prioritizing vocabulary expansion and open-source regional corpus collection during the pre-training stage to enhance AI inclusivity and fluency.

Chemistry, environmental health, and occupational health have historically developed in close collaboration. This study aimed to evaluate the performance of LLMs, in responding to a chemistry course questionnaire used in environmental and occupational health department for educational purposes. This was a cross-sectional study conducted in 2026. The study used a 50-item multiple-choice questionnaire, primarily in Persian with limited English terms and formulas, which was administered to LLMs (ChatGPT-5.5, Gemini 3, and Copilot 2026). Performance was evaluated using confusion matrix analysis. Cochran`s Q test, McNemar`s test for pair-wise comparisons, and Point-biserial correlation were also conducted to further evaluate the study data. The LLMs presented mean sensitivity, specificity, and accuracy of 0.81, 0.29, and 0.68, respectively. Gemini 3 presented a high level of performance, achieving the highest sensitivity (0.85), specificity (0.56), and accuracy (0.80). ChatGPT-5.5 had the lowest sensitivity (0.76), while Copilot showed the lowest specificity (0.07) and an accuracy of 0.62. No significant correlations were found between performance and questionnaire characteristics; however, all models performed poorly on negatively framed items requiring identification of incorrect options. The study presented some preliminary insights on the performance of LLMs in chemistry-related questions. Further research is warranted.

documents.abstract: Welding quality inspection of battery top covers is critical to lithium-ion battery safety and reliability. The height deviation between weld defects and normal areas is extremely small; on specular, weakly textured surfaces it produces no stable brightness contrast, so two-dimensional (2D) images carry almost no usable defect signal. Three-dimensional (3D) sensing captures such deviations but incurs computational costs prohibitive for production lines. Raw depth maps, as scalar grayscale fields, cause 2D convolutional networks to overlook tiny-defect features. Addressing all three limitations simultaneously remains a key challenge for artificial intelligence (AI) in industrial inspection. To address this challenge, we propose a geometry-to-photometry defect detection framework that converts 3D weld geometry into discriminative 2D photometric representations via physically inspired rendering. Depth data are first mapped to pseudo-color images, and surface normals then modulate lighting under a Phong-based model to transform subtle geometric discontinuities into high-contrast photometric cues. Building on this strategy, we develop YOLO-WaveletTiny (YOLO-WT), a lightweight You Only Look Once (YOLO) detector integrating wavelet depthwise separable convolution and inverse wavelet upsampling for efficient feature extraction and reconstruction. Experiments on a real industrial dataset with six defect categories show the rendered representation improves the baseline by 5.9 percentage points in mean average precision at 50% intersection over union (mAP@50), and the full framework achieves 93.8% mAP@50 with only 2.47 million parameters and 5.7 GFLOPs, outperforming mainstream detectors. These results demonstrate the framework as an effective, practical AI solution for low-cost, high-precision weld defect inspection.
topics: Industrial Vision Systems and Defect Detection

documents.abstract: Project narrative for a proposed pilot study of a large language model (LLM)-based conversational agent that administers the PHQ-9 and the Columbia Suicide Severity Rating Scale (C-SSRS) to prenatal and postnatal patients in an outpatient setting. This is a grant narrative (a research plan), not a report of results: no data have been collected. Posted as is; names of people, partner institutions and the funder have been removed. The reference list is included. Abstract: The project plans to pilot test a functional prototype conversational agent with human-in-the-loop safety, using a participatory development approach (workshops, interviews and feedback surveys) and Agile development, to evaluate user experience, therapeutic alliance, performance and accuracy, and to inform a future clinical trial.
topics: Maternal Mental Health During Pregnancy and Postpartum
Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Accurate agricultural yield prediction is crucial for crop management and data-driven decision-making. This study proposes a machine learning framework for predicting total lentil seed yield using 264 observations collected during a single growing season at one location in Sivas, Türkiye. Seven regression models and the tabular foundation model TabPFN were evaluated through nested cross-validation. The fixed post hoc Foundation-Augmented Averaging Ensemble (FAAE) combined TabPFN, Extra Trees, CatBoost, and XGBoost using equal weights, while the primary fully nested evaluation selected the four ensemble members within each outer training fold. The fully nested FAAE achieved R2 = 0.891 ± 0.045, comparable to the strongest individual models, while the fixed post hoc FAAE yielded R2 = 0.897 ± 0.038. Split conformal prediction produced well-calibrated uncertainty intervals at 80%, 90%, and 95% coverage. SHAP and LOCO identified pods per plant and biological yield as the dominant predictors of lentil yield. Overall, these findings indicate that FAAE can provide competitive predictive performance within a leakage-controlled framework while also supporting uncertainty quantification and biologically meaningful interpretation. Because the dominant predictors, pods per plant and biological yield, are measured at or near physiological maturity, the proposed framework is more suitable for end-of-season yield estimation than for early-season forecasting. The framework therefore shows potential for within-trial yield assessment, although validation using replicated material across additional years and locations is required before broader generalization.

Predictive policing based on artificial intelligence is shifting crime prevention from reactive response toward data-driven risk identification, pattern recognition, and resource prioritization. This transformation creates a legal dilemma: the same systems that may improve analytical capacity can also amplify historical bias, enable opaque profiling, intrude upon privacy, and influence coercive decisions without adequate procedural safeguards. This article analyzes the legal position of predictive policing in Indonesia and formulates a rights-based governance model for police use of artificial intelligence. The research applies normative juridical analysis using statutory, conceptual, comparative, and policy approaches. The analysis focuses on the 2022 Personal Data Protection Law, the 2023 Criminal Code, the 2025 Criminal Procedure Code, the 2026 amendment to the Police Law, and Indonesia's emerging national AI governance framework. The study finds that Indonesia already possesses fragmented legal bases relevant to AI-supported policing, but lacks a dedicated risk-based framework that defines prohibited uses, high-risk systems, human oversight, auditability, contestability, and allocation of responsibility. The article proposes a four-layer governance model: constitutional safeguards, statutory legality, AI governance controls, and operational human review. Predictive outputs should function as decision-support rather than autonomous grounds for coercive action.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Introduction:Teachers form the backbone of any educational system, shaping future generations through constant interaction and communication.In the Indian context, where classroom resources are often limited, the teacher's voice becomes the most vital instructional tool.However, prolonged and excessive voice use places teachers at considerable risk of vocal discomfort, presenting as dryness, hoarseness, throat irritation, and voice fatigue.These symptoms not only hinder effective teaching but also affect teachers' well-being, productivity, and overall quality of education.Despite its significance, vocal health remains a largely overlooked occupational concern among school teachers, particularly at the primary level.Recognizing this gap, the present study was undertaken to explore the magnitude of vocal discomfort among primary school teachers.Material and method A non-experimental descriptive research design was adopted for the study.A total of 200 primary school teachers from selected schools in the Sangli-Miraj-Kupwad Corporation area were included using a cluster sampling technique.Data was collected using the standardized Vocal Tract Discomfort Scale (VTDS) developed by Mathieson, administered in both Marathi and English for better comprehension.The tool comprised two sections: demographic variables and an 8-item self-rating scale assessing frequency and severity of vocal discomfort symptoms on a 6-point Likert scale.The total score ranged from 0 to 96 and was categorized into no, normal, mild, moderate, and extreme levels of vocal discomfort.Content validity was established by 20 experts, ensuring the tool's appropriateness for the study setting. Results:The findings revealed a notable burden of vocal discomfort among teachers.Symptoms such as dryness (46%), aching (43.5%), and soreness (39.5%) were commonly reported, followed by tightness (34%) and burning sensations (31.5%).Overall, most participants experienced mild (65%) to moderate (35%) levels of discomfort.The prevalence of vocal discomfort was found to be 45.56%.Female teachers constituted a larger proportion of the sample, and most participants had 1-10 years of teaching experience, with an average daily teaching duration of 5-6 hours. Conclusion:The study highlights that nearly half of the primary school teachers experience some degree of vocal discomfort, underscoring it as a significant occupational health issue.Although vocal discomfort appears to be influenced by demographic and work-related factors, no statistically significant association was observed in this study.These findings emphasize the need for early screening, awareness programs, and preventive voice care strategies to safeguard teachers' vocal health and enhance their professional efficiency.

Abstract Air pollution is identified by the World Health Organisation (WHO) as the leading environmental threat to human health, with indoor exposure particularly concerning given its daily, long-term nature. Europeans spend approximately 90% of their time indoors, where poor indoor air quality (IAQ) contributes an estimated 2 million disability-adjusted life-years lost annually in the EU, with vulnerable populations especially at risk. This study explores a Knowledge Graph (KG) as a decision-support tool to prioritise Substances of Concern (SoC) for indoor dust and air. Two complementary approaches were applied: a top-down screening that filters a broad substance universe against defined criteria to identify monitoring candidates, and a bottom-up characterisation of already monitored substances against the same criteria. Integrating publicly available chemical data within the KG and applying a risk-oriented approach based on hazard classification, REACH registration tonnage and use information, we narrowed a list of over 16,000 substances (PlastChem list) down to 42. This work shows that KG can effectively connect diverse data sources and identified both known and emerging SoC not yet monitored in private settings. It highlights that non-REACH chemicals may contribute significantly to indoor dust chemistry analysis, and REACH consumer-use data alone does not capture all uses relevant to residential indoor exposure. The experiments show that expanding the number and diversity of integrated data sources is recommended to refine scoping for chemical monitoring, risk assessment and management. Key concerns among identified substances include reproductive toxicity and respiratory tract irritation, often linked to numerous consumer products. The ECHA Classification and Labelling Inventory was found to be a useful hazardous substance pool, though further refinement with additional health-related data is recommended. Finally, we discuss how integrating Large Language Models (LLMs) and KG into the framework could support partial automation of the validation of SoC, improving future monitoring and analysis efficiency.
topics: Indoor Air Quality and Microbial Exposure

documents.abstract: Human inquiry has developed through philosophy, mathematics, physics, biology, logic, psychology, cognitive science, religious studies, and numerous other disciplines. Each investigates particular aspects of existence through its own concepts, methods, and standards of explanation. Yet the relationships among these domains raise a fundamental question: Can a common structural framework help us understand how different forms of organisation emerge, persist, transform, and become intelligible to observers within reality? Recursive Structural Reality (RSR) proposes such a framework through the interconnected concepts of existence, difference, relation, structure, information, transformation, recursion, stability, persistence, and identity. Its central proposition, Identity = Stable Recursion, directs attention towards the processes through which recognisable organisation may persist despite changes in components, states, or circumstances. RSR also investigates the conditions under which structures lose stability, undergo transformation, reorganise, and give rise to new forms of organisation. A second foundational dimension concerns the observer. Human beings do not investigate reality from outside the universe but participate in the reality they seek to understand. Through perception, memory, language, logic, mathematics, and reflection, observers construct models that organise experience and make particular aspects of existence intelligible. These models are indispensable to knowledge, yet they remain selective representations whose assumptions, limitations, and domains of validity require examination. The scope of RSR extends from foundational ontology and mathematical structures to physical systems, biological organisation, intelligence, artificial intelligence, consciousness, knowledge, religious traditions, and social institutions. These domains provide different contexts in which questions about structure, transformation, stability, persistence, and identity can be investigated. Their inclusion within a common framework does not imply that they share identical mechanisms or can be explained through one undifferentiated model. Each application requires concepts, methods, and standards of evidence appropriate to its subject. RSR therefore distinguishes philosophical RSR, mathematical RSR, and physical RSR while situating them within a broader interdisciplinary research programme. Philosophical coherence, mathematical derivation, and physical validity are related but distinct requirements. Similarly, applications to biological, cognitive, religious, and social phenomena require their own explanatory development and appropriate forms of investigation. This paper establishes the conceptual foundations, expanded scope, methodological orientation, and research architecture of RSR. It presents the framework as an evolving programme whose contributions must be assessed through conceptual precision, formal development, explanatory value, and empirical or comparative investigation. Its long-term objective is an integrated understanding of reality that investigates structural connections across domains without erasing their differences, while examining both the phenomena under investigation and the limitations of the models through which they are understood.

Purpose This study aims to examine how three dimensions of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI), namely, capability, application and knowledge modelling, are associated with entrepreneurial innovation, and whether innovation mediates their associations with entrepreneurial performance and entrepreneurial success in startups and small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs). Design/methodology/approach Survey data from 317 startup and SME owners, partners and employees were analysed using confirmatory factor analysis followed by AMOS-based structural path analysis in IBM SPSS analysis of moment structures (AMOS) 20.0 with maximum likelihood estimation. Specific indirect effects were assessed using bias-corrected bootstrapping with 5,000 resamples and 95% confidence intervals. Findings All three GenAI dimensions were positively associated with entrepreneurial innovation, with knowledge modelling showing the largest reported association. Entrepreneurial innovation was positively associated with performance and success, and all six specific indirect associations were significant. The largest reported indirect associations were observed for knowledge modelling. Research limitations/implications The cross-sectional, single-source design supports associations rather than causal claims. Practical implications Entrepreneurs should prioritise knowledge-related practices, verification of AI-generated information and human judgement rather than treating tool use alone as evidence of innovation. Policy and support programmes should develop these practices alongside access to GenAI tools. Originality/value The study distinguishes GenAI capability, application and knowledge modelling within one entrepreneurial model and examines entrepreneurial innovation as a mediating knowledge-conversion pathway linking these dimensions with performance and success.

As digital technologies become increasingly embedded in organizational processes, understanding the determinants of continued technology usage, particularly in AI-augmented digital workplaces, is essential for optimizing employee engagement and performance. This study evaluates continuance intentions in AI-augmented remote work systems by extending the Expectation Confirmation Model (ECM) with constructs such as perceived enjoyment, trust in technology, self-efficacy, and user satisfaction. Using Structural Equation Modeling (SEM) on data from 348 experienced users of digital work platforms, our analysis reveals that trust and perceived enjoyment significantly influence satisfaction, which in turn drives continued usage intentions. Notably, the dynamics of remote work technology adoption diverge from prior information systems continuance models, with enjoyment and psychological assurance playing more prominent roles than traditionally modeled constructs like utility alone. These findings highlight the evolving expectations of knowledge workers in AI-enabled work environments, where user-centric design, intelligent automation, and trustworthy system behaviors are paramount. The study offers actionable insights for system designers and digital transformation leaders seeking to sustain user engagement in an increasingly hybrid and AI-integrated workplace. The results provide important implications for organizations designing or deploying digital collaboration tools.

Background. Artificial intelligence (AI) now mediates much of science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM) learning, yet adoption has outpaced theory. The tension is whether AI scaffolding relieves cognitive burden or performs the self-regulatory work autonomy requires, and implementation varies too widely for a single average to describe. Objectives. This review estimates the pooled effect of AI scaffolding on STEM achievement and self-regulated learning, tests whether technological paradigm moderates that effect, and asks whether the literature can evaluate learning after support is withdrawn. Methods. Under PRISMA 2020, four platforms searched in October 2026 (spanning 2021–2026) yielded 21,819 records; 13,786 unique records were dual-screened into an 83-record corpus, then 41 extracted cohorts. Each contributes one harmonised contrast (k = 29; N = 3,709), so within-study dependence is structurally absent. Effects were pooled by two-level random-effects meta-analysis fitted with restricted maximum likelihood and Knapp–Hartung adjustment. Results. The pooled effect was Hedges g = 0.8045 (95% CI [0.5469, 1.0621]), with τ² = 0.4410 and I² = 92.78%. The 95% prediction interval [−0.5846, 2.1936] spans zero, and no moderator reached significance. Notably, 27 of 29 cohorts (93.1%) never withdrew support, and none measured unassisted performance after removal. Conclusions. AI scaffolding yields a large but implementation-dependent gain, consistent with extraneous-load offloading rather than cognitive substitution. The decisive finding is the shape of the evidence base: the field measured a human-AI system in assembly and stayed silent on the competence of the human alone. We name this evidentiary void the Autonomy Gap. Keywords: artificial intelligence; self-regulated learning; STEM education; scaffolding fading; cognitive load theory; transfer of responsibility; meta-analysis; evidence synthesis
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning
